nodes.name: Hidden characterization of polyhedral convex sets (Banakh-Hetman)
nodes.statement: In \cite{BH} the authors proved that a closed convex subset $C$ of a complete linear metric space $X$ is polyhedral in its linear hull if and only if $C$ hides no infinite subset $A\subset X\setminus C$ in the sense that $[a,b]\cap C\ne\emptyset$ for any distinct points $a,b\in A$.
assumptions: a closed convex subset $C$ of a complete linear metric space $X$
conclusions: is polyhedral in its linear hull if and only if $C$ hides no infinite subset $A\subset X\setminus C$ in the sense that $[a,b]\cap C\ne\emptyset$ for any distinct points $a,b\in A$
equivalent_conditions: is polyhedral in its linear hull
$C$ hides no infinite subset $A\subset X\setminus C$ in the sense that $[a,b]\cap C\ne\emptyset$ for any distinct points $a,b\in A$
also_stated_at: By \cite{BH}, a closed convex subset $C$ of a complete linear metric space $X$ is hiding if and only if $C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull.
nodes.statement_short: A closed convex set in a complete linear metric space is polyhedral in its linear hull iff it hides no infinite set outside it.

nodes.name: Space of closed convex sets with the Hausdorff metric
nodes.statement: For a Banach space $X$ by $\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X)$ we denote the space of all non-empty closed convex subsets of $X$, endowed with the {\em Hausdorff metric} $$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,B)=\max\{\sup_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,B),\sup_{b\in B}\mathsf{dist}(b,A)\}\in[0,\infty].$$
nodes.genus: space of all non-empty closed convex subsets of $X$
nodes.statement_short: Conv_H(X) is the hyperspace of non-empty closed convex subsets of X with the (possibly infinite) Hausdorff metric.

nodes.name: Distance from a point to a set
nodes.statement: Here $\mathsf{dist}(a,B)=\inf\limits_{b\in B}\|a-b\|$ stands for the distance from a point $a\in X$ to a subset $B\subset X$ of the Banach space $X$.

nodes.name: Hausdorff distance is a metric on a component
nodes.statement: It is well-known that for each closed convex set $C\in\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X)$ the Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt$ restricted to the set $$\mathcal H_C=\{A\in\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X):\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,C)<\infty\}$$is a metric, see \cite[Ch2]{Sendov}.
assumptions: each closed convex set $C\in\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X)$
conclusions: the Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt$ restricted to the set $$\mathcal H_C=\{A\in\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X):\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,C)<\infty\}$$is a metric
nodes.statement_short: The Hausdorff distance restricted to the sets at finite distance from C is a genuine (finite) metric.

nodes.name: Hausdorff metric component
nodes.statement: The obtained metric space $(\mathcal H_C,\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt)$ will be called the {\em Hausdorff metric component} (or just {\em component}) of the set $C$ in $\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X)$.

nodes.name: Closed half-space, polyhedral and approximatively polyhedral convex sets
nodes.statement: A convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ is called \begin{itemize} \item {\em a closed half-space} if $C=f^{-1}([a,+\infty)$ for some non-zero linear continuous functional $f:X\to\mathbb R$ and some real number $a\in\mathbb R$; \item {\em polyhedral} if $C$ can be written as the intersection $C=\cap \mathcal F$ of a finite family $\mathcal F$ of closed half-spaces in $X$; \item {\em approximatively polyhedral} if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a closed polyhedral subset $P\subset X$ that lies on Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)<\varepsilon$ from $C$. \end{itemize}
nodes.genus: convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
nodes.statement_short: Half-space = superlevel set of a nonzero functional; polyhedral = finite intersection of half-spaces; approximatively polyhedral = Hausdorff-approximable by polyhedral sets.

nodes.name: The whole space is polyhedral
nodes.statement: Observe that the whole space $X$ is polyhedral, being the intersection $X=\cap\mathcal F$ of the empty family $\mathcal F=\emptyset$ of closed half-spaces.

nodes.name: Compact convex sets are approximatively polyhedral
nodes.statement: It is well-known that each compact convex subset of Banach space is approximatively polyhedral (see \cite{Gruber} for more information on that topic).
conclusions: each compact convex subset of Banach space is approximatively polyhedral

nodes.name: Convex parabola and convex hyperbola
nodes.statement: This is not necessarily true for non-compact closed convex sets. For example, the convex parabola $$P=\big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y\ge x^2\big\}$$is not approximatively polyhedral in $\mathbb R^2$, while the convex hyperbola $$H=\big\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y\ge \sqrt{x^2+1}\big\}$$is approximatively polyhedral.
nodes.statement_short: The parabola y>=x^2 is not approximatively polyhedral while the hyperbola y>=sqrt(x^2+1) is.

nodes.name: Set hiding another set
nodes.statement: Following \cite{BH}, we say that a subset $C$ of a linear space $X$ {\em hides} a set $A\subset X$ if for any two distinct points $a,b\in A$ the affine segment $[a,b]=\{ta+(1-t)b:t\in[0,1]\}$ meets the set $C$.
differentia: for any two distinct points $a,b\in A$ the affine segment $[a,b]=\{ta+(1-t)b:t\in[0,1]\}$ meets the set $C$

nodes.name: Hiding, positively hiding and infinitely hiding convex sets
nodes.statement: A convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ is called \begin{itemize} \item {\em hiding} if $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$; \item {\em positively hiding} if $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$ such that $\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)>0$; \item {\em infinitely hiding} if $C$ hides some infinite set $A\subset X\setminus C$ such that $\sup_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)=\infty$. \end{itemize}
nodes.genus: convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$
nodes.statement_short: C is hiding if it hides an infinite set outside it; positively/infinitely hiding if that set can be at positive inf / infinite sup distance from C.

nodes.name: Infinitely hiding implies positively hiding implies hiding
nodes.statement: It is clear that each infinitely hiding set is positively hiding and each positively hiding set is hiding.
conclusions: each infinitely hiding set is positively hiding
each positively hiding set is hiding

nodes.name: Hiding properties of the parabola and the hyperbola
nodes.statement: So, both parabola and hyperbola are hiding (being not polyhedral). Yet, the parabola is infinitely hiding (but not approximatively polyhedral) while the hyperbola is not positively hiding (but is approximatively polyhedral).

nodes.name: Characteristic cone
nodes.statement: Let us recall that the {\em characteristic cone} of a convex subset $C$ in a linear topological space $X$ is the set $V_C$ of all vectors $v\in X$ such that for every point $c\in C$ the ray $c+\bar {\mathbb R}_+v=\{c+tv:t\ge 0\}$ lies in $C$.
differentia: for every point $c\in C$ the ray $c+\bar {\mathbb R}_+v=\{c+tv:t\ge 0\}$ lies in $C$
also_stated_at: Let us recall that for a convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ its {\em characteristic cone} $V_C$ is defined by $$V_C=\{x\in X:\forall c\in C\;\;c+\bar{\mathbb R}_+x\subset C\}\subset X.$$

nodes.name: Closed half-line
nodes.statement: Here $\bar {\mathbb R}_+=[0,\infty)$ denotes the closed half-line.

nodes.name: Characteristic cone of a closed or open set is closed
nodes.statement: The characteristic cone $V_C$ is closed in $X$ if $C$ is closed or open in $X$, see Lemma~\ref{l2.2n}.
assumptions: $C$ is closed or open in $X$
conclusions: The characteristic cone $V_C$ is closed in $X$

nodes.name: Klee's characterization in finite dimensions
nodes.statement: In finite-dimensional case, the equivalence of the conditions (1)--(3) was proved by Viktor Klee in \cite{Klee}.
conclusions: In finite-dimensional case, the equivalence of the conditions (1)--(3) was proved by Viktor Klee in \cite{Klee}
nodes.statement_short: In finite dimensions, conditions (1)-(3) of Theorem 1.1 are equivalent (Klee).

nodes.name: Hidden characterization of approximatively polyhedral convex sets
nodes.statement: For a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ the following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $C$ is approximatively polyhedral; \item the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ is polyhedral in $X$ and $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)<\infty$; \item the component $\mathcal H_C$ contains a polyhedral closed convex set; \item the component $\mathcal H_C$ contains no positively hiding closed convex set; \item the space $\mathcal H_C$ is separable; \item the space $\mathcal H_C$ has density $\mathrm{dens}(\mathcal H_C)<\mathfrak c$. \end{enumerate} If the Banach space $X$ is finite-dimensional, then the conditions (1)--(6) are equivalent to: \begin{enumerate} \item[(7)] $C$ is not positively hiding; \item[(8)] $C$ is not infinitely hiding. \end{enumerate}

the Banach space $X$ is finite-dimensional
conclusions: the following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $C$ is approximatively polyhedral; \item the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ is polyhedral in $X$ and $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)<\infty$; \item the component $\mathcal H_C$ contains a polyhedral closed convex set; \item the component $\mathcal H_C$ contains no positively hiding closed convex set; \item the space $\mathcal H_C$ is separable; \item the space $\mathcal H_C$ has density $\mathrm{dens}(\mathcal H_C)<\mathfrak c$. \end{enumerate}
the conditions (1)--(6) are equivalent to: \begin{enumerate} \item[(7)] $C$ is not positively hiding; \item[(8)] $C$ is not infinitely hiding. \end{enumerate}

conclusions: the conditions (1)--(6) are equivalent to: \begin{enumerate} \item[(7)] $C$ is not positively hiding; \item[(8)] $C$ is not infinitely hiding. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement_short: For closed convex C in a Banach space: approximatively polyhedral <=> polyhedral characteristic cone at finite distance <=> H_C separable <=> H_C has no positively hiding set, etc.; in finite dimensions also <=> C not positively/infinitely hiding.
nodes.label: main

nodes.name: Density of a topological space
nodes.statement: Let us recall that the {\em density} $\mathrm{dens}(X)$ of a topological space $X$ is the smallest cardinality $|D|$ of a dense subset $D$ of $X$.

nodes.name: Separable space
nodes.statement: Topological spaces with at most countable density are called {\em separable}.

nodes.name: Unit ball of l_2 is positively but not infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: Observe that the closed unit ball $C=\{x\in l_2:\|x\|\le 1\}$ in the separable Hilbert space $l_2$ is positively hiding but not infinitely hiding. This example shows that the conditions $(7)$ and $(8)$ are not equivalent in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces.

nodes.name: Real scalars
nodes.statement: All linear (and Banach) spaces considered in this paper are over the field of real numbers $\mathbb R$.

nodes.name: Convex cone
nodes.statement: By a {\em convex cone} in a linear space $X$ we understand a convex subset $C\subset X$ such that $tc\in C$ for any $t\in\bar{\mathbb R}_+$ and $c\in C$.
differentia: $tc\in C$ for any  $t\in\bar{\mathbb R}_+$ and $c\in C$

nodes.name: Open half-line
nodes.statement: Here $\bar {\mathbb R}_+=[0,+\infty)$ stands for the closure of the open half-line $\mathbb R_+=(0,+\infty)$ in $\mathbb R$.

nodes.name: Pointwise sum and homothetic copy
nodes.statement: For two subsets $A,B$ of a linear space $X$ and a real number $\lambda$, let $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\;b\in B\}$ be the pointwise sum of $A$ and $B$, and $\lambda A=\{\lambda\cdot a:a\in A\}$ be a homothetic copy of $A$.

nodes.name: Cone generated by a set
nodes.statement: Each subset $F\subset X$ generates the cone $$\mathrm{cone}(F)=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_ix_i:\mbox{$n\in\mathbb N$ and $(x_i)_{i=1}^n\in F^n$, $(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^n\in\bar{\mathbb R}_+^n$}\Big\},$$which contains the convex hull $\mathrm{conv}(F)$ of $F$.

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional description of polyhedral cones and sets (Minkowski-Weyl)
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional Banach space. \begin{enumerate} \item A convex cone $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\mathrm{cone}(F)$ for some finite set $F\subset X$. \item A convex set $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\mathrm{cone}(F)+\mathrm{conv}(E)$ for some finite sets $F,E\subset X$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $X$ be a finite-dimensional Banach space
A convex cone $C\subset X$
A convex set $C\subset X$
conclusions: A convex cone $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\mathrm{cone}(F)$ for some finite set $F\subset X$.
A convex set $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\mathrm{cone}(F)+\mathrm{conv}(E)$ for some finite sets $F,E\subset X$.

assumptions: A convex cone $C\subset X$
conclusions: A convex cone $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\mathrm{cone}(F)$ for some finite set $F\subset X$.

assumptions: A convex set $C\subset X$
conclusions: A convex set $C\subset X$ is polyhedral if and only if $C=\mathrm{cone}(F)+\mathrm{conv}(E)$ for some finite sets $F,E\subset X$.

nodes.name: Dual characteristic cone
nodes.statement: By the {\em dual characteristic cone} of $C$ we understand the convex cone $$V_C^*=\{x^*\in X^*:\sup x^*(C)<\infty\}$$lying in the dual Banach space $X^*$.

nodes.name: Dual characteristic cone of a set equals that of its closure
nodes.statement: It is clear that the dual characteristic cone $V_C^*$ of a convex set $C\subset X$ coincides with the dual characteristic cone $V_{\bar C}^*$ of its closure $\bar C$ in $X$.
conclusions: the dual characteristic cone $V_C^*$ of a convex set $C\subset X$ coincides with the dual characteristic cone $V_{\bar C}^*$ of its closure $\bar C$ in $X$

nodes.name: Characteristic cone of the closure
nodes.statement: Let $\bar C$ be the closure of a convex set $C$ in a Banach space $X$. Then \begin{enumerate} \item $V_C\subset V_{\bar C}$; \item $V_C=V_{\bar C}$ if the set $C$ is open in $X$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $\bar C$ be the closure of a convex set $C$ in a Banach space $X$
the set $C$ is open in $X$
conclusions: $V_C\subset V_{\bar C}$
$V_C=V_{\bar C}$
$V_C\subset V_{\bar C}$

assumptions: the set $C$ is open in $X$
conclusions: $V_C=V_{\bar C}$

nodes.name: Points at prescribed distance along a non-characteristic direction
nodes.statement: For each point $c_0$ of a convex set $C$ in a Banach space $X$, each vector $v\notin V_{\bar C}$ and each real number $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_+$ there is a real number $t\in\mathbb R_+$ such that $\mathsf{dist}(c_0+tv,C)=\varepsilon$.
assumptions: each point $c_0$ of a convex set $C$ in a Banach space $X$
each vector $v\notin V_{\bar C}$
each real number $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_+$

nodes.name: Sets at finite Hausdorff distance have equal characteristic cones
nodes.statement: Let $A,B$ be two closed convex sets in a Banach space $X$. If $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,B)<\infty$, then $V_A=V_B$.
assumptions: $A,B$ be two closed convex sets in a Banach space $X$
$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,B)<\infty$
conclusions: $V_A=V_B$
nodes.label: l2.4n

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4
nodes.statement: We lose no generality assuming that $0\in A\cap B$. If $V_A\ne V_B$, then we can find a vector $v\in X$ that lies in $V_A\setminus V_B$ or in $V_B\setminus V_A$. We lose no generality assuming that $v\in V_B\setminus V_A$. By Lemma~\ref{l2.3}, there is a positive real number $t$ such that $\mathsf{dist}(tv,A)>\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,B)$, which is not possible as $tv\in V_B\subset B$.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a direction in V_B but not V_A gives, by Lemma 2.3, points of B arbitrarily far from A.

nodes.name: Inclusion of dual characteristic cones
nodes.statement: Observe that for a convex $C$ containing zero, the inclusion $V_C\subset C$ implies $V_C^*\subset V^*_{V_C}$.
assumptions: a convex $C$ containing zero
conclusions: the inclusion $V_C\subset C$ implies $V_C^*\subset V^*_{V_C}$

nodes.name: Dual cone of the characteristic cone is a weak* closure
nodes.statement: For any closed convex set $C$ in a Banach space the dual characteristic cone $V^*_{V_C}$ of the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ coincides with the weak$^*$ closure $\mathrm{cl}^*(V_C)$ of $V_C$.
assumptions: any closed convex set $C$ in a Banach space
conclusions: the dual characteristic cone $V^*_{V_C}$ of the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ coincides with the weak$^*$ closure $\mathrm{cl}^*(V_C)$ of $V_C$
nodes.label: l2.5n

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.5
nodes.statement: We lose no generality assuming that $0\in C$. Observe that the dual characteristic cone $$V^*_{V_C}=\{x^*\in X^*:\sup x^*(V_C)<\infty\}=\{x^*\in X^*:\sup x^*(V_C)=0\}=\bigcap_{v\in V_C}\{x^*\in X^*:x^*(v)\le 0\}$$is weak$^*$ closed in $X^*$, being an intersection of weak$^*$-closed half-spaces in $X^*$. So, the inclusion $V^*_C\subset V^*_{V_C}$ implies $\mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)\subset V^*_{V_C}$. It remains to prove the reverse inclusion $V^*_{V_C}\subset \mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)$. Assume conversely that it is not true and find a functional $x^*\in V^*_{V_C}\setminus\mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)$. By the Hahn-Banach Theorem applied to the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$, there is an element $x\in X$ that separates $x^*$ from $\mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)$ in the sense that $$x^*(x)>\sup\{v^*(x):v^*\in\mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)\}\ge\sup\{v^*(x):v^*\in V^*_C\}.$$ We claim that $v^*(x)\le 0$ for all functionals $v^*\in V^*_C$. Assuming that $v^*(x)>0$, we can find a positive real number $\lambda$ so large that $\lambda v^*(x)>x^*(x)$, which contradicts the choice of $x$ (because $\lambda v^*\in V^*_C$). So, $v^*(x)\le 0$ for all $v^*\in V^*_C$. We claim that $x\in V_C$. In the opposite case, we could find a positive real number $t>0$ such that $tx\notin C$ (here we recall that $0\in C$). Applying Hahn-Banach Theorem, find a linear functional $v^*\in X^*$ such that $v^*(tx)>\sup v^*(C)\ge 0$. Then $v^*\in V^*_C$ and $v^*(x)>0$, which contradicts the property of $x$ established at the end of the preceding paragraph. This contradiction shows that $x\in V_C$ and then $x^*(x)>0$ implies that $\sup x^*(V_C)=\infty$, which contradicts the choice of the functional $x^*\in V^*_{V_C}$. This contradiction completes the proof of the inclusion $V^*_{V_C}\subset \mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)$.
nodes.statement_short: One inclusion since V*_{V_C} is weak*-closed; the reverse by contradiction, separating with Hahn-Banach in the weak* topology.

nodes.name: Polyhedral sets lie near their characteristic cones
nodes.statement: The following lemma implies that polyhedral convex sets in Banach spaces lie on positive Hausdorff distance from their characteristic cones.
conclusions: polyhedral convex sets in Banach spaces lie on positive Hausdorff distance from their characteristic cones

nodes.name: Hausdorff distance between a polyhedral set and its characteristic cone
nodes.statement: For a normed space $X$, functionals $f_1,\dots,f_n:X\to\mathbb R$, a vector $\mathbf a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb R^n$ with non-negative coordinates, and the polyhedral convex set $$P_{\mathbf a}=\bigcap\limits_{i=1}^nf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big)$$ \begin{enumerate} \item the characteristic cone $V_{P_{\mathbf a}}$ of the convex set $P_{\mathbf a}$ coincides with the polyhedral cone $P_{\mathbf 0}$; \item $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf a},P_{\mathbf 0})\le \mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 1})\cdot\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}a_i$, \end{enumerate} where $\mathbf 0=(0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)$.
assumptions: a normed space $X$
functionals  $f_1,\dots,f_n:X\to\mathbb R$
a  vector $\mathbf a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb R^n$ with non-negative coordinates
conclusions: the characteristic cone $V_{P_{\mathbf a}}$ of the convex set $P_{\mathbf a}$ coincides with the polyhedral cone $P_{\mathbf 0}$
$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf a},P_{\mathbf 0})\le \mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 1})\cdot\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}a_i$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.6
nodes.statement: We consider the space $\mathbb R^n$ as a Banach lattice with coordinatewise operations of minimum and maximum. \smallskip 1. The first statement is easy and is left to the reader as an exercise. \smallskip 2. To prove the second statement, we first check that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 1})<\infty$. By Lemma~\ref{l2.1}(2), $P_{\mathbf 1}=\mathrm{conv}(F)+\mathrm{cone}(E)$ for some finite sets $F,E\subset X$. It follows that the cone $\mathrm{cone}(E)$ coincides with the characteristic cone $P_{\mathbf 0}$ of $P_{\mathbf 1}$ and hence $P_{\mathbf 1}=\mathrm{conv}(F)+P_{\mathbf 0}$. Then $$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\mathrm{conv}(F)+P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\mathrm{conv}(F),\{0\})<\infty.$$ Let $a=\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}a_i$. Taking into account that that the norm of the Banach space $X$ is homogeneous and that $P_{\mathbf 0}\subset P_{\mathbf a}\subset P_{a\mathbf 1}$, we get the required inequality $$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf a},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{a\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})=a\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})\cdot \max_{1\le i\le n}a_i<\infty.$$
nodes.statement_short: Part 1 left to the reader; for part 2, write P_1=conv(F)+P_0 via Lemma 2.1 and use homogeneity with P_0 within P_a within P_{a1}.

nodes.name: Klee's lemma: countable dense polyhedral family in finite dimensions
nodes.statement: If the component $\mathcal H_C$ of a closed convex subset $C$ of a finite-dimensional Banach space $X$ contains a polyhedral convex set, then $\mathcal H_C$ contains a countable dense family of polyhedral convex sets.
assumptions: the component $\mathcal H_C$ of a closed convex subset $C$ of a finite-dimensional Banach space $X$ contains a polyhedral convex set
conclusions: $\mathcal H_C$ contains a countable dense family of polyhedral convex sets
nodes.label: l3.1

nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Quotient Banach space and quotient operator
nodes.statement: Let us recall that for a Banach space $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ and a closed linear subspace $Z\subset X$, the quotient Banach space $Y=X/Z$ is endowed with the norm $$\|y\|_Y=\inf\big\{\|x\|_X:x\in q^{-1}(y)\big\},$$ where $q:X\to Y$, $q:x\mapsto x+Z$, stands for the quotient operator.
nodes.statement_short: X/Z carries the quotient norm inf of norms over the coset; q:x->x+Z is the quotient operator.

nodes.name: Induced operator on closed convex sets
nodes.statement: The quotient operator $q:X\to Y$ induces an operator $\bar{q}:\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X)\to\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(Y)$ assigning to each closed convex set $C\subset X$ the closure $\bar qC$ of its image $qC$ in the Banach space $Y$.

nodes.name: Quotient maps and closed convex sets
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ be a closed linear subspace of a Banach space $X$, $Y=X/Z$ be the quotient Banach space, and $q:X\to Y$ be the quotient operator. \begin{enumerate} \item A convex set $C\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_C$ is closed in $X$ if and only if the image $qC$ is closed in $Y$. \item A convex set $C\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_C$ is polyhedral in $X$ if and only if its image $qC$ is polyhedral in $Y$. \item For any non-empty convex sets $A,B\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_A\cap V_B$ we get $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,B)=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(qA,qB)$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $Z$ be a closed linear subspace of a Banach space $X$
$Y=X/Z$ be the quotient Banach space
$q:X\to Y$ be the quotient operator
conclusions: A convex set $C\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_C$ is closed in $X$ if and only if the image $qC$ is closed in $Y$.
A convex set $C\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_C$ is polyhedral in $X$ if and only if its image $qC$ is polyhedral in $Y$.
For any non-empty convex sets $A,B\subset X$ with $Z\subset V_A\cap V_B$ we get $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,B)=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(qA,qB)$.
nodes.statement_short: If Z lies in the characteristic cones, the quotient map preserves closedness, polyhedrality and Hausdorff distance.
nodes.label: l3.3

nodes.name: Components containing a polyhedral set are separable
nodes.statement: If the component $\mathcal H_C$ of a non-empty closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ contains a polyhedral convex set, then $\mathcal H_C$ contains a countable dense family of polyhedral closed sets, which implies that the space $\mathcal H_C$ is separable and the convex set $C$ is approximatively polyhedral.
assumptions: the component $\mathcal H_C$ of a non-empty closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ contains a polyhedral convex set
conclusions: $\mathcal H_C$ contains a countable dense family of polyhedral closed sets
the space $\mathcal H_C$ is separable
the convex set $C$ is approximatively polyhedral
nodes.label: l3.4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement: The statement of the lemma is trivial if $C=X$. So, we assume that $C\ne X$ and $\mathcal H_C$ contains a polyhedral convex set $P$. Replacing $P$ by its shift, we can assume that $0\in P$. Write $P$ as a finite intersection of closed half-spaces $$P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big),$$ where $f_1,\dots,f_k:X\to\mathbb R$ are suitable linear continuous functionals and $a_1,\dots,a_k$ are suitable non-negative real numbers. It follows from $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)<\infty$ that the characteristic cone $$V_C=V_P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big)$$ is polyhedral and the closed linear subspace $$Z=-V_C\cap V_C=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}(0)$$has finite codimension in $X$. Then the quotient Banach space $Y=X/Z$ is finite-dimensional. Taking into account that $Z\subset V_P\cap V_C$ and applying Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(1,3), we conclude that the images $qC$ and $qP$ are closed convex sets in $Y$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(qC,qP)<\infty$. Moreover, the convex set $qP$ is polyhedral in $Y$. Since the Banach space $Y$ is finite-dimensional, it is legal to apply Lemma~\ref{l3.1} in order to find a dense countable subset $\mathcal D_Y\in\mathcal H_{qC}$ that consists of polyhedral convex sets. By Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(2), the countable family $\mathcal D_X=\{q^{-1}(D):D\in\mathcal D_X\}$ consists of polyhedral convex subsets of $X$ and by Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(3) is dense in the component $\mathcal H_C$ of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Quotient by the lineality space Z of V_C (finite codimension) and transfer the finite-dimensional Lemma 3.1 back via Lemma 3.3.

nodes.name: Hiding is preserved under convex hulls with C
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a convex subset of a linear space $X$ and $a,b\in X$ two points such that $[a,b]\cap C\ne\emptyset$. Then for any points $x\in\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})$ and $y\in\mathrm{conv}(X\cup\{b\})$ we get $[x,y]\cap C\ne\emptyset$.
assumptions: $C$ be a convex subset of a linear space $X$
$a,b\in X$ two points such that $[a,b]\cap C\ne\emptyset$
conclusions: for any points $x\in\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})$ and $y\in\mathrm{conv}(X\cup\{b\})$ we get $[x,y]\cap C\ne\emptyset$
nodes.label: l4.1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: The lemma trivially holds if $x$ or $y$ belongs to the set $C$. So, we assume that $x,y\notin C$. It follows that the point $x\in\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})\setminus C$ can be written as $x=t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x$ for some $t_x\in(0,1]$ and $c_x\in C$. The same is true for the point $y\in\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{b\})\setminus C$ which can be written as $y=t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y$ for some $t_y\in(0,1]$ and $c_y\in C$. By our assumption, the intersection $[a,b]\cap C$ contains some point $c=ta+(1-t)b$ where $t\in[0,1]$. The lemma will be proved as soon as we check that the segment $[x,y]$ meets the convex hull $\mathrm{conv}(\{c,c_x,c_y\})\subset C$ of the 3-element set $\{c,c_x,c_y\}\subset C$. This will follow as soon as we find real numbers $u,\alpha,\alpha_x,\alpha_y\in[0,1]$ such that $\alpha+\alpha_x+\alpha_y=1$ and $$\alpha c+\alpha_xc_x+\alpha_yc_y=ux+(1-u)y=u(t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x)+(1-u)(t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y).$$ The number $u\in[0,1]$ can be found from the equation $$ut_xa+(1-u)t_yb=(ut_x+(1-u)t_y)(ta+(1-t)b)=(ut_x+(1-u)t_y)c,$$ which has a well-defined solution $$u=\frac{t\cdot t_y}{t\cdot t_y+(1-t)t_x}.$$ The remaining numbers $\alpha,\alpha_x$ and $\alpha_y$ can be found as $$\alpha=ut_x+(1-u)t_y,\quad \alpha_x=u(1-t_x),\quad\alpha_y=(1-u)(1-t_y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Explicitly solve for convex coefficients showing a point of [x,y] lies in conv{c,c_x,c_y}, contained in C.

nodes.name: Positively hiding sets force non-separable components
nodes.statement: The component $\mathcal H_C\subset\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X)$ of a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ has density $\mathrm{dens}(\mathcal H_C)\ge\mathfrak c$ provided $\mathcal H_C$ contains a positively hiding closed convex subset $P$ of $X$.
assumptions: $\mathcal H_C$ contains a positively hiding closed convex subset $P$ of $X$
conclusions: The component $\mathcal H_C\subset\mathrm{Conv}_{\mathsf H}(X)$ of a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ has density $\mathrm{dens}(\mathcal H_C)\ge\mathfrak c$
nodes.label: l4.2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal H_C=\mathcal H_P$, we lose no generality assuming that the convex set $C$ itself is positively hiding, which means that there is an infinite subset $A\subset X\setminus C$ on positive distance $\varepsilon=\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)$ from $C$, which is hidden behind the set $C$ in the sense that for any distinct points $a,b\in A$ the affine segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$. Fix any point $c_0\in C$ and for every point $a\in A$ choose a point $b_a\in[c_0,a]$ on the distance $\mathsf{dist}(b_a,C)=\varepsilon$ from $C$. The choice of the point $b_a$ is possible as $\mathsf{dist}(a,C)\ge\varepsilon$. Lemma~\ref{l4.1} guarantees that the set $B=\{b_a:a\in A\}$ is infinite and is hidden behind the set $C$. Moreover, this set lies in the $2\varepsilon$-neighborhood $C+2\varepsilon\mathbb B$ of $C$. Here $\mathbb B=\{x\in X:\|x\|< 1\}$ stands for the open unit ball in the Banach space $X$. Now for any subset $\beta\subset B$ consider the convex set $C_\beta=\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\beta)$. Applying Lemma~\ref{l4.1} one can show that this set is closed in $X$ and $C_\beta=\bigcup_{b\in\beta}\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{b\})$. Taking into account that $C\subset C_\beta\subset C+2\varepsilon\mathbb B$, we see that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,C_\beta)\le 2\varepsilon$ and hence $C_\beta$ belongs to the component $\mathcal H_C$ of $C$. We claim that for any two distinct subsets $\alpha,\beta\subset B$, the convex sets $C_\alpha$ and $C_\beta$ lie on the Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\alpha,C_\beta)\ge\varepsilon$. Since $\alpha\ne\beta$, there is a point $b\in (\beta\setminus\alpha)\cup(\alpha\setminus\beta)$. We lose no generality assuming that $b\in\beta\setminus\alpha$. Then $b\in C_\beta$ and $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$. Indeed, assuming that $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)<\varepsilon$, we conclude that the open $\varepsilon$-ball $b+\varepsilon\mathbb B$ meets the set $C_\alpha=\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\alpha)=\bigcup_{a\in \alpha}\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})$ at some point $x$ that belongs to $\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})$ for some point $a\in\alpha$. Since the set $B\ni a,b$ is hidden behind the set $C$, the segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$. By Lemma~\ref{l4.1}, the segment $[x,b]$ also meets the set $C$, which is not possible as $[x,b]$ lies in the $\varepsilon$-ball $b+\varepsilon \mathbb B$, which does not meet $C$ as $\mathsf{dist}(b,C)=\varepsilon$. This contradiction shows that $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$ and hence $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\beta,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$. Now we see that the component $\mathcal H_C$ contains the subset $\mathcal C=\{C_\beta:\beta\subset B\}$ of cardinality $|\mathcal C|\ge 2^{|B|}\ge\mathfrak c$, consisting of points on mutual distance $\ge \varepsilon$. This implies that $\mathrm{dens}(\mathcal H_C)\ge |\mathcal C|\ge \mathfrak c$.
nodes.statement_short: From a hidden set B at distance eps, the sets conv(C with beta), beta a subset of B, form 2^|B| points of H_C at mutual distance at least eps.

nodes.name: C-infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: Let $C_0,C$ be two convex sets in a Banach space $X$. We shall say that $C_0$ is {\em $C$-infinitely hiding} if $C_0$ hides some infinite set $A\subset\mathrm{aff}(C_0)$ such that $\sup_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)=\infty$.
differentia: $C_0$ hides some infinite set $A\subset\mathrm{aff}(C_0)$ such that $\sup_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)=\infty$

nodes.name: Infinitely hiding iff C-infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that a convex set $C\subset X$ is infinitely hiding if and only if it is $C$-infinitely hiding.
conclusions: a convex set $C\subset X$ is infinitely hiding if and only if it is $C$-infinitely hiding

nodes.name: Hiding cones are C-infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: Let $C\ni 0$ be a convex set in a Banach space and $V_{\bar C}$ be the characteristic cone of its closure. For a linear subspace $Z\subset X$, the intersection $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is $C$-infinitely hiding if the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is a hiding convex set in $Z$.
assumptions: $C\ni 0$ be a convex set in a Banach space
the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is a hiding convex set in $Z$
conclusions: the intersection $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is $C$-infinitely hiding
nodes.label: l5.1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: Assume that the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ hides some infinite injectively enumerated set $\{a_n\}_{n\in\omega}\subset Z\setminus V_{\bar C}$. By Lemma~\ref{l2.3}, for every $n\in\omega$, there is a real number $t_n>0$ such that $\mathsf{dist}(t_n a_n,C)>n$. It is clear that for the set $A=\{t_na_n\}_{n\in\omega}$ we get $\sup\limits_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\mathsf{dist}(t_na_n,C)=\infty$. It remains to show that for every distinct numbers $n,m\in\omega$ the segment $[t_na_n,t_mb_m]$ intersects the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$. Since the set $\{a_n,a_m\}\subset A\subset Z$ is hidden behind $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$, the segment $[a_n,a_m]$ meets the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ at some point $c=\tau a_n+(1-\tau)a_m$ where $\tau\in[0,1]$. Then for the number $$u=\frac{\tau t_m}{\tau t_m+(1-\tau)t_n}\in[0,1]$$we get $$ ut_na_n+(1-u)t_ma_m=\frac{t_nt_n}{\tau t_m+(1-\tau)t_n}(\tau a_n+(1-\tau)a_m)=\frac{t_nt_m}{\tau t_m+(1-\tau)t_n}c\in [t_na_n,t_ma_m]\cap V_{\bar C} $$and hence the intersection $Z\cap V_{\bar C}\cap[t_na_n,t_ma_m]\ni ut_na_n+(1-u)t_ma_m$ is not empty.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale the hidden points a_n by Lemma 2.3 so they escape C, and check the rescaled segments still meet the cone.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2 from the Banakh-Hetman characterization
nodes.statement: By \cite{BH}, a closed convex subset $C$ of a complete linear metric space $X$ is hiding if and only if $C$ is polyhedral in its closed linear hull. This characterization combined with Lemma~\ref{l5.1} implies:
nodes.statement_short: Combine the Banakh-Hetman hiding characterization with Lemma 5.1.

nodes.name: Characteristic cone sections and C-hiding
nodes.statement: Let $C\ni 0$ be a convex set in a Banach space and $V_{\bar C}$ be the characteristic cone of its closure. For a closed linear subspace $Z\subset X$ the intersection $V=Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is infinitely $C$-hiding if the cone $V$ is polyhedral in its closed linear hull $V^\pm=\mathrm{cl}(V-V)$.
assumptions: $C\ni 0$ be a convex set in a Banach space
the cone $V$ is polyhedral in its closed linear hull $V^\pm=\mathrm{cl}(V-V)$
conclusions: the intersection $V=Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ is infinitely $C$-hiding
nodes.label: l5.2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: This lemma implies its absolute version:
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 5.2 with Z the whole space.

nodes.name: Non-polyhedral characteristic cone implies infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: A closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space is infinitely hiding if its characteristic cone $V_C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull $V_C^\pm=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$.
assumptions: its characteristic cone $V_C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull $V_C^\pm=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$
conclusions: A closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space is infinitely hiding
nodes.label: l5.3

nodes.name: Lifting hidden sets through a linear map
nodes.statement: Let $q:X\to \tilde X$ be a linear operator between linear spaces, $E=q^{-1}(0)$ be the kernel of $q$, and $C\subset X$ be a convex set such that $V_{C\cap E}-V_{C\cap E}=E$. If the image $\tilde C=q(C)$ hides some countable set $\tilde A\subset \mathrm{aff}(\tilde C)$, then $C$ hides some set $A\subset \mathrm{aff}(C)$ with $q(A)=\tilde A$.
assumptions: $q:X\to \tilde X$ be a linear operator between linear spaces
$C\subset X$ be a convex set such that $V_{C\cap E}-V_{C\cap E}=E$
the image $\tilde C=q(C)$ hides some countable set $\tilde A\subset \mathrm{aff}(\tilde C)$
conclusions: $C$ hides some set $A\subset \mathrm{aff}(C)$ with $q(A)=\tilde A$
nodes.label: l5.4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement:

nodes.name: C-infinite hiding from quotient images
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a Banach space, $E$ be a closed linear subspace of $X$, $\tilde X=X/E$ be the quotient Banach space and $q:X\to \tilde X$ be the quotient operator. Let $C_0,C$ be two convex sets in $X$ and $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$, $\tilde C=q(C)$ be their quotient images in $\tilde X$. The convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding $X$ if its image $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding and $E=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$.
assumptions: its image $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding
$E=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$
conclusions: The convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding $X$
nodes.label: l5.5

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement: If $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding, then $\tilde C_0$ hides some infinite set $\tilde A\subset \mathrm{aff}(\tilde C_0)$ such that $\sup_{\tilde a\in \tilde A}\mathsf{dist}(\tilde a,\tilde C)=\infty$. By Lemma~\ref{l5.4}, there is a set $A\subset \mathrm{aff}(C_0)$ with $q(A)=\tilde A$, hidden behind the set $C$. Since the quotient operator $q:X\to \tilde X$ has norm $\|q\|\le 1$, for every point $a\in A$ and its image $\tilde a=q(a)$, we get $\mathsf{dist}(\tilde a,\tilde C)\le \mathsf{dist}(a,C)$. Consequently, $\sup_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)\ge \sup_{\tilde a\in \tilde A}\mathsf{dist}(\tilde a,\tilde C)=\infty$, which means that the set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding.
nodes.statement_short: Lift the hidden set by Lemma 5.4; since the quotient map is non-expanding, distances to C stay unbounded.

nodes.name: Two-dimensional sections far from their cones are C-infinitely hiding
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a closed convex subset of a Banach space $X$ and $Z$ be a two-dimensional linear subspace of $X$ such that the convex set $C\cap Z$ has non-empty interior $C_0$ in $Z$, which contains zero. If $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$, then the convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding.
assumptions: $C$ be a closed convex subset of a Banach space $X$
$Z$ be a two-dimensional linear subspace of $X$ such that the convex set $C\cap Z$ has non-empty interior $C_0$ in $Z$, which contains zero
$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$
conclusions: the convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.6
nodes.statement:
The equality $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that the open convex subset $C_0$ of the plane $Z$ is not bounded. Consequently, its characteristic cone $V_{C_0}=V_{ ar C_0}=Z\cap V_C$ is unbounded too. Moreover, the cone $V_{C_0}$ is not a plane, not a half-plane, and not a line (otherwise $C_0$ would be on finite Hausdorff distance from its characteristic cone $V_{C_0}$). We lose no generality assuming that $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$. If $V_{C_0}=\mathrm{cone}(\{e_1\})$, then the equality $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$ or $\sup e_2^*(C_0)=+\infty$. Changing $e_2$ to $-e_2$, if necessary, we can assume that $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$. So, in both cases we can assume that $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$. e\emptyset$ for all $k<n$. \end{enumerate} We start the inductive construction selecting a point $a_0\in\mathbb R_+\cdot(e_1-e_2)$ on the distance $\mathsf{dist}(a_0,C)>0$ from the set $C$. Such point $a_0$ exists because $e_1-e_2

To derive a contradiction, assume that $C_0$ is not $C$-infinitely hiding. In this case Lemma~ef{l5.6} implies the following fact, which will be used several times in the subsequent proof.  egin{claim} For each two-dimensional linear subspace $Z_2\subset Z$ we get $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(Z_2\cap C_0,V_{Z_2\cap C_0})<\infty$. \end{claim} Now consider the characteristic cone $V_{C_0}=V_{ ar C_0}$ of the open convex set $C_0$ in $Z$.  egin{claim} The linear subspace $-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is trivial. \end{claim}  egin{proof} Assume that the linear subspace $E=-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is not equal to $\{0\}$. Consider the quotient Banach space $	ilde X=X/E$, the quotient operator $q:X	o 	ilde X$, the convex set $	ilde C=q(C)$, and the finite-dimensional subspace $	ilde Z=q(Z)$ of dimension $\dim(	ilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. Since the quotient operator $q|Z:Z	o	ilde Z$ is open, the convex set $	ilde C_0=q(C_0)$ is open in $	ilde Z$ and hence the convex set $	ilde Z\cap	ilde C$ has non-empty interior in $	ilde Z$. Since $E\subset V_C$, the set $	ilde C$ is closed in the Banach space $	ilde X$ by Lemma~ef{l3.3}(1). Now we can see that the triple $(	ilde X,	ilde C,	ilde Z)$ satisfies the requirements of Lemma~ef{l5.7} with $\dim(	ilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. So, by the inductive assumption, the convex set $	ilde C_0$ is $	ilde C$-infinitely hiding. Since $E=V_{E\cap C_0}=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$, we can apply Lemma~ef{l5.4} to conclude that the open convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding in $X$. But this contradicts our assumption. \end{proof}  egin{claim} $\dim(V_{C_0})\ge 2$. \end{claim}  egin{proof} Assume conversely that $\dim(V_{C_0})\le 1$. The equality $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that the open convex subset $C_0$ is unbounded in the finite-dimensional linear space $Z\cap C_0$ and consequently $V_{C_0}
e 0$. Since $-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}=\{0\}$, we conclude that $V_{C_0}= ar{\mathbb R}_+ e$ for some non-zero vector $e\in V_{C_0}$. Now consider the linear subspace $E=\mathbb R e\subset Z$, the quotient Banach space $	ilde X=X/E$, the finite-dimensional linear subspace $	ilde Z=q(Z)$, the convex sets $	ilde C=q(C)$, and the open convex set $	ilde C_0=q(C_0)$, which is dense in $	ilde C$. Claim~ef{cl5.8} guarantees that the set $	ilde C_0$ has trivial characteristic cone and hence is bounded in the finite-dimensional space $	ilde Z$. We shall assume that the number $k$ in this representation is the smallest possible. e i\}$ is strictly larger than $V_{C_0}$ and hence contains a point $x\in V\setminus V_{C_0}$. For this point $x$ we get $f_j(x)\le 0$ for all $j
e i$, and $f_i(x)>0$. Since $\dim(V_{C_0})\ge 2$, there exists a vector $y\in V_{C_0}\setminus\mathbb R x$. Such choice of $x$ guarantees that $0

On the other hand, the projection $q(Z_2\cap C)$ contains the half-line $\mathbb R_+ w$, which implies that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(Z_2\cap C,V_{Z_2\cap C})=\infty$. But this contradicts Claim~ef{cl5.8}. \end{proof} Taking into account that $\infty=\sup f_i(C_0)=\sup 	ilde f_i(	ilde C_0)$, we conclude that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(	ilde C_0,V_{	ilde C_0})=\infty$ and by the inductive assumption, the open convex set $	ilde C_0$ is $	ilde C$-infinitely hiding (as $\dim(	ilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$). nodes.statement_short: A cone direction w with positive f_i would give a two-dimensional section at infinite distance from its cone, contradicting Claim 5.8.

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional affine sections far from the cone give infinite hiding
nodes.statement: A closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ is infinitely hiding if $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A\cap C,A\cap V_C)=\infty$ for some finite-dimensional affine subspace $A\subset X$.
assumptions: $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A\cap C,A\cap V_C)=\infty$ for some finite-dimensional affine subspace $A\subset X$
conclusions: A closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ is infinitely hiding
nodes.label: l5.8

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.13
nodes.statement: It is well-known that $C\cap A$ has non-empty interior $C_0$ in its affine hull $\mathrm{aff}(C\cap A)$. Moreover, $C\cap A$ coincides with the closure $\bar C_0$ of $C_0$ in $A$. Shifting the set $C$, if necessary, we can assume that $0\in C_0$. Then $Z=\mathrm{aff}(C_0)$ is a finite-dimensional linear subspace of $X$ such that $C\cap Z=C\cap A$ has non-empty interior $C_0$ which contains zero and is dense in $C\cap Z$. It follows that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(Z\cap C,V_{Z\cap C})=\infty$ and hence $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding by Lemma~\ref{l5.7}, and $C$ is infinitely hiding as $C_0\subset C$.
nodes.statement_short: Shift so that 0 lies in the relative interior of the section and apply Lemma 5.7.

nodes.name: Biorthogonal sequence
nodes.statement: We recall that a sequence of pairs $\{(x_n,x^*_n)\}_{n\in \omega}\subset X\times X^*$ is {\em biorthogonal} if $x^*_n(x_n)=1$ and $x^*_n(x_k)=0$ for all $n\ne k$, see \cite[1.1]{HMVZ}.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets

nodes.name: Bounded biorthogonal sequences in the dual characteristic cone
nodes.statement: Assume that a closed convex subset $C$ of an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ has trivial characteristic cone $V_C=\{0\}$. Then there exists a biorthogonal sequence $\{(x_n,x_n^*)\}_{n\in\omega}\subset X\times V^*_C$ such that $\|x^*_n\|=1\le \|x_n\|<4$ for all $n\in\omega$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
assumptions: a closed convex subset $C$ of an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ has trivial characteristic cone $V_C=\{0\}$
conclusions: there exists a biorthogonal sequence $\{(x_n,x_n^*)\}_{n\in\omega}\subset X\times V^*_C$ such that $\|x^*_n\|=1\le \|x_n\|<4$ for all $n\in\omega$
nodes.label: l6.1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: Replacing $C$ by a shift of its closed neighborhood, we can assume that the convex subset $C$ of $X$ has non-empty interior $C_0$, which contains zero. After such replacement the cones $V_C$ and $V_C^*$ will not change, see Lemma~\ref{l2.4n}. The biorthogonal sequence $\{(x_n,x_n^*)\}_{n\in\omega}$ will be constructed by induction. We start by choosing an arbitrary functional $x^*_0\in V^*_C$ and a point $x_0\in X$ with $1=\|x_0^*\|=x^*_0(x_0)\le \|x_0\|<4$. Assume that for some $k\in\omega$ a finite biorthogonal sequence $\{(x_n,x^*_n)\}_{n<k}\subset X\times V^*_C$ has been constructed so that $1=\|x^*_n\|\le\|x_n\|<4$ for all $n< k$. Let $L^*$ be the linear hull of the finite set $\{x^*_0,\dots,x^*_{k-1}\}$ in the dual Banach space $X^*$. In the compact set $L^*_2=\{x^*\in L:\|x^*\|\le 2\}$, choose a finite subset $F^*_2\subset L^*_2$ such that for each functional $x^*\in L^*_2$ there is a functional $y^*\in F^*_2$ with $\|x^*-y^*\|<\frac18$. For every functional $f\in F^*_2$ choose a point $x_f\in X$ such that $\|x_f\|=1$ and $f(x_f)>\|f\|-\frac18$. Let $E$ be the linear hull of the finite set $\{x_i:i<k\}\cup\{x_f:f\in F_2^*\}$ in $X$. Let $\tilde X=X/E$ be the quotient Banach space, $q:X\to\tilde X$ be the quotient operator, and $\tilde C=q(C)$ be the quotient image of the convex set $C$ in $\tilde X$. Since the quotient operator $q$ is open, the image $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ coincides with the interior of $\tilde C$ in $\tilde X$. We claim that the set $\tilde C_0$ has trivial characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}=\{0\}$. Assuming the converse, find a non-zero vector $\tilde v\in V_{\tilde C_0}$, choose any vector $v\in q^{-1}(\tilde v)$ and consider the finite-dimensional linear subspace $E_v=\mathrm{lin}(E\cup\{v\})$. The triviality of the characteristic cone $V_C=\{0\}$ implies that the intersection $E_v\cap C_0$ is bounded and then the image $q(E_v\cap C_0)=\mathbb R \tilde v\cap \tilde C_0$ also is bounded. So, $\bar{\mathbb R}_+\tilde v\not\subset C_0$, which contradicts $\tilde v\in V_{\tilde C_0}\setminus\{0\}$. The triviality of the cone $V_{\tilde C_0}=\{0\}$ implies that $\tilde C\ne \tilde X$, so we can find a functional $\tilde x_k^*\in V^*_{\tilde C_0}$ with unit norm $\|\tilde x_k^*\|=1$. Now consider the functional $x_k^*=\tilde x_k^*\circ q$ and observe that $\|x_k^*\|=\|\tilde x^*_k\|=1$ and $x_k^*(x_i)=0$ for all $i<k$ and $x_k^*(x_f)=0$ for all $f\in F_2^*$. We claim that $\mathsf{dist}(x^*_k,L^*)>\frac14$. Assuming the converse, find a functional $l^*\in L^*$ with $\|x^*_k-l^*|\le \frac14$. Then $\|l^*\|\le\|x^*_k\|+\frac14$, so $l^*\in L_2^*$ and by the choice of the set $F_2^*$, we can find a functional $f\in F^*_2$ such that $\|l^*-f\|<\frac18$. Then $\|x^*_k-f\|\le\|x^*_k-l^*\|+\|l^*-f\|\le \frac14+\frac18=\frac38$, $\|f\|\ge\|x^*_k\|-\|x^*_k-f\|\ge 1-\frac38=\frac58$ and we obtain the contradiction: $$\frac48=\frac58-\frac18\le \|f\|-\frac18<f(x_f)=|x_k^*(x_f)-f(x_f)|\le\|x^*_k-f\|\cdot\|x_f\|\le\frac38.$$ This contradiction shows that $\mathsf{dist}(x^*_k,L^*)>\frac14$ and implies that the the closed $\frac14$-ball $B^*=\{x^*\in X^*:\|x^*-x^*_{k}\|\le \frac14\}$ centered at $x^*_{k}$ does not intersect $L^*$. By the Banach-Alaoglu Theorem this ball is compact in the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$. Now the Hahn-Banach Theorem applied to the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$ yields us a point $x_{k}\in X$ that separates $L^*$ and $B^*$ in the sense that $\sup_{x^*\in L^*}x^*(x_{k})< \inf_{x^*\in B^*}x^*(x_{k})$. It follows from the linearity of $L^*$ that $x^*(x_{k})=0$ for all $x^*\in L^*$. In particular, $x^*_i(x_{k})=0$ for all $i< k$. Multiplying $x_{k}$ by a suitable positive constant, we may additionally assume that $x^*_{k}(x_{k})=1$. Then $\|x_{k}\|\ge 1$ because $x^*_{k}$ has unit norm. To finish the inductive step it suffices to check that $\|x_k\|<4$. Assuming the converse, find a functional $x^*\in X^*$ with unit norm such that $x^*(x_k)=\|x_k\|\ge 4$. Then the functional $y^*=x^*_k-\frac14x^*$ belongs to the ball $B^*$ and thus $y^*(x_k)>0$. On the other hand, $y^*(x_k)=x^*_k(x_k)-\frac14x^*(x_k)\le 1-\frac14\cdot4= 0$, which is a desired contradiction.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Inductive construction: quotient by a finite-dimensional space to find a new unit functional in V*_C far from the span of the previous ones, then separate by Hahn-Banach and Banach-Alaoglu.

nodes.name: Approximation by positively hiding sets when the characteristic cone is trivial
nodes.statement: Assume that a closed convex subset $C$ of an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ has trivial characteristic cone $V_C=\{0\}$. Then for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positively hiding closed convex set $C_\varepsilon\subset X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)\le \varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
assumptions: a closed convex subset $C$ of an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ has trivial characteristic cone $V_C=\{0\}$
conclusions: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positively hiding closed convex set $C_\varepsilon\subset X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)\le \varepsilon$
nodes.label: l6.2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l6.1}, there exists a biorthogonal sequence $\{(x_n,x_n^*)\}_{n\in\omega}\subset X\times V^*_C$ such that $1=\|x_n^*\|\le \|x_n\|<4$ for all $n\in\omega$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$, a positively hiding convex set $C_\varepsilon$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)\le\varepsilon$ can be defined by the formula: $$C_\varepsilon=\big\{x\in \mathrm{cl}(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B):\forall n\in\omega\;\;x^*_n(x)\le \tfrac18\varepsilon+\sup x^*_n(C)\big\}$$where $\mathbb B=\{x\in X:\|x\|<1\}$ stands for the open unit ball of the Banach space $X$. It is clear that $C\subset C_\varepsilon\subset \mathrm{cl}(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B)$, which implies that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C,C)\le\varepsilon$. It remains to check that the set $\tilde C$ is positively hiding. This can be done as follows. For every $n\in\omega$ choose a point $c_n\in C$ with $x^*_n(c_n)>\sup x^*_n(C)-\tfrac1{16}\varepsilon$ and consider the point $a_n=c_n+\frac{\varepsilon}4 x_n$. We claim that $\mathsf{dist}(a_n,C_\varepsilon)\ge \frac1{16}\varepsilon$. Indeed, for any point $c\in C_\varepsilon$, we get $x^*_n(c)\le\sup x^*_n(C)+\frac18\varepsilon$ while $$x^*_n(a_n)=\frac\varepsilon4 x^*_n(x_n)+x^*_n(c_n)>\frac\varepsilon4+\sup x^*_n(C)-\frac\varepsilon{16}=\frac{3\varepsilon}{16}+\sup x^*_n(C).$$ Consequently, $\|a_n^*-c\|=\|x^*_n\|\cdot\|a_n-c\|\ge x^*_n(a_n)-x^*(c)\ge \frac{3\varepsilon}{16}-\frac{\varepsilon}{8}=\frac\varepsilon{16}$. So, the set $A=\{a_n\}_{n\in\omega}$ lies on positive distance $\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C_\varepsilon)\ge\frac1{16}\varepsilon$ from $C_\varepsilon$. To show that the set $A$ is infinite and hidden behind $C_\varepsilon$, it suffices to check that for any distinct numbers $n,m$ the midpoint $\frac12a_n+\frac12a_m$ of the segment $[a_n,a_m]$ belongs to the convex set $C_\varepsilon$. Taking into account that $a_n,a_m\subset \mathrm{cl}(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B)$, we conclude that $\frac12a_n+\frac12a_m\in [a_n,a_m]\subset \mathrm{cl}(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B)$. The inclusion $\frac12a_n+\frac12a_m\in C_\varepsilon$ will follow from definition of $C_\varepsilon$ as soon as we check that $x^*_k(\frac12a_n+\frac12a_m)\le\sup x^*_k(C)+\frac18\varepsilon$ for every $k\in\omega$. If $k\notin\{n,m\}$, then $x^*_k(x_n)=x^*_k(x_m)=0$ and hence $$x^*_k(\tfrac12a_n+\tfrac12a_m)=x^*_k(\tfrac12c_n+\tfrac12c_m)\le\sup x^*_k(C).$$ If $k=n$, then $$x^*_k(\tfrac12a_n+\tfrac12a_m)=x^*_n(\tfrac12c_n+\tfrac12c_m)+\tfrac18\varepsilon x^*_n(x_n)\le\sup x^*_n(C)+\tfrac18\varepsilon.$$By analogy we can treat the case $k=m$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Cut the eps-neighbourhood of C by the half-spaces of the biorthogonal functionals and show the points c_n+(eps/4)x_n are hidden at distance eps/16.

nodes.name: Approximation by positively hiding sets for infinite-codimensional cone span
nodes.statement: Assume that for a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ the closed linear subspace $Z=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$ has infinite codimension in $X$. Then for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positively hiding convex set $C_\varepsilon\subset X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)\le \varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
assumptions: for a closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ the closed linear subspace $Z=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$  has infinite codimension in $X$
conclusions: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positively hiding convex set $C_\varepsilon\subset X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)\le \varepsilon$
nodes.label: l6.3

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.3
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{l3.3} (by analogy with the proof of Lemma~\ref{l3.4}), we can reduce the proof to the case $-V_C\cap V_C=\{0\}$. So, from now on we assume that $-V_C\cap V_C=\{0\}$. Replacing $C$ by a shift of its closed neighborhood, we can assume that $C$ has non-empty interior $C_0$ in $X$ and $0\in C_0$. If the characteristic cone $V_C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull $Z=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$, then by Lemma~\ref{l5.3}, the convex set $C$ is infinitely (and hence positively) hiding and hence we can put $C_\varepsilon=C$. So, we assume that the characteristic cone $V_C$ is polyhedral in $Z$. Since $-V_C\cap V_C=\{0\}$, the polyhedrality of $V_C$ implies that the closed linear space $Z=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$ is finite-dimensional and coincides with $V_C-V_C$. Now consider the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/Z$, the quotient operator $q:X\to\tilde X$, and the convex set $\tilde C=q(C)$. Since the operator $q$ is open, the image $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ of the interior $C_0$ of $C$ coincides with the interior of $\tilde C$. Now consider the characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}$ of the open convex set $\tilde C_0$. If $V_{\tilde C_0}$ contains some non-zero vector $\tilde v$, then for any vector $v\in q^{-1}(v)$ and for the finite-dimensional linear subspace $E=\mathrm{lin}(Z\cup\{v\})$ the intersection $E\cap C_0$ lies on infinite Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(E\cap C_0,V_{E\cap C_0})=\infty$ from its characteristic cone. This is so because $q(V_{E\cap C_0})\subset q(V_C)=\{0\}$ while $q(E\cap C_0)\supset\bar{\mathbb R}_+\tilde v$. Then Lemma~\ref{l5.8} guarantees that the set $C$ is infinitely (and hence positively) hiding. In this case we can put $C_\varepsilon=C$. So, it remains to consider the case $V_{\tilde C_0}=\{0\}$. In this case, Lemma~\ref{l6.2} yields a positively hiding closed convex set $\tilde C_\varepsilon\subset\tilde X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C_\varepsilon,\tilde C_0)<\varepsilon$. Now consider the convex set $C_\varepsilon=(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B)\cap q^{-1}(\tilde C_\varepsilon)$ and observe that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)\le\varepsilon$ and $q(C_\varepsilon)=\tilde C_\varepsilon$. The set $\tilde C_\varepsilon$, being positively hiding, hides a countably infinite set $\tilde A\subset \tilde X\setminus\tilde C_\varepsilon$ on positive distance $\inf_{a\in\tilde A}\mathsf{dist}(a,\tilde C_\varepsilon)>0$ from $\tilde C_\varepsilon$. Taking into account that $Z=V_{Z\cap C_0}-V_{Z\cap C_0}$ and $q(C_\varepsilon)=\tilde C_\varepsilon$, with help of Lemma~\ref{l5.4}, we can find an infinite subset $A\subset q^{-1}(\tilde A)$ hidden behind the convex set $C_\varepsilon\subset C$. Since the quotient operator $q$ is not expanding, the set $A$ lies on positive distance $$\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)=\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C_0)\ge\inf_{\tilde a\in\tilde A}\mathsf{dist}(\tilde a,\tilde C_0)>0$$from the convex set $C_\varepsilon$. So, $C_\varepsilon$ is positively hiding.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a pointed polyhedral cone, quotient by its span, and either get infinite hiding by Lemma 5.13 or approximate the quotient by Lemma 6.2 and lift by Lemma 5.4.

nodes.name: Approximation by positively hiding sets when far from the characteristic cone
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a closed convex set in a Banach space $X$. If $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)=\infty$, then for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positively hiding convex set $\tilde C\subset X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C,C)\le \varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
assumptions: $C$ be a closed convex set in a Banach space $X$
$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)=\infty$
conclusions: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positively hiding convex set $\tilde C\subset X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C,C)\le \varepsilon$
nodes.label: l6.4

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.4
nodes.statement: If the closed linear subspace $V_C^\pm=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$ has infinite codimension in $X$, then the existence of a positively hiding convex set $C_\varepsilon\subset X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)<\varepsilon$ follows from Lemma~\ref{l6.3}. So, we assume that $V^\pm_C$ has finite codimension in $X$. If the characteristic cone $V_C$ is not polyhedral in $V_C^\pm$, then the set $C$ is infinitely (and positively) hiding by Lemma~\ref{l5.3}. In this case we can put $C_\varepsilon=C$. It remains to consider the case of polyhedral cone $V_C$ in $V_C^\pm$. Since $V_C^\pm$ has finite codimension in $X$, the characteristic cone $V_C$ is polyhedral in $X$ and hence the closed linear subspace $V^\mp_C=-V_C\cap V_C$ has finite codimension in $X$. Then the quotient Banach space $Y=X/V^\mp_C$ is finite-dimensional. Let $q:X\to Y$ be the quotient operator. Lemma~\ref{l3.3} guarantees that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(qC,V_{qC})=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)=\infty$ and then the set $qC$ is infinitely hiding in $Y$ by Lemma~\ref{l5.8}. By Lemma~\ref{l5.5}, the set $C$ is infinitely (and hence positively) hiding in $X$. Letting $C_\varepsilon=C$, we finish the proof of the lemma.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the codimension and polyhedrality of the cone, using Lemmas 6.3, 5.3, 5.13 and 5.5.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: To prove the first part of Theorem~\ref{main}, for every closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ we should prove the equivalence of the following conditions: \begin{enumerate} \item $C$ is approximatively polyhedral; \item the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ is polyhedral in $X$ and $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)<\infty$; \item $\mathcal H_C$ contains a polyhedral closed convex set; \item $\mathcal H_C$ contains no positively hiding closed convex set; \item the space $\mathcal H_C$ is separable; \item the space $\mathcal H_C$ has density $\mathrm{dens}(\mathcal H_C)<\mathfrak c$. \end{enumerate} It suffices to prove the implications $(1)\Rightarrow(2)\Rightarrow(3)\Rightarrow(5)\Rightarrow(6)\Rightarrow(4)\Rightarrow(2)\Rightarrow(3)\Rightarrow(1)$, among which $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$ and $(5)\Rightarrow(6)$ are trivial. The remaining implications can be established as follows. \smallskip To prove the implication $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$, assume that the closed convex set $C$ is approximatively polyhedral and find a polyhedral convex set $P$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)<\infty$. Lemma~\ref{l2.4n} implies that $V_C=V_P$. The polyhedral convex set $P$ can be written as a finite intersection $P=\bigcap_{i=1}^n f_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big)$ of closed hyperplanes determined by some functionals $f_1,\dots,f_n:X\to\mathbb R$ and some real numbers $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R$. It is easy to check that $$V_C=V_P=\bigcap_{i=1}^n f_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big),$$ which means that the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ is polyhedral. By Lemma~\ref{l2.6}, $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P,V_C)=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P,V_P)<\infty$. Consequently, $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)\le \mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)+\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P,V_C)<\infty$. \smallskip The implications $(3)\Rightarrow(5)$ and $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$ are proved in Lemma~\ref{l3.4} and $(6)\Rightarrow(4)$ in Lemmas~\ref{l4.2}. The implication $(4)\Rightarrow(2)$ follows from Lemmas~\ref{l5.3}, \ref{l6.3} and \ref{l6.4}. Next, assuming the Banach space is finite-dimensional we will check that the conditions (1)--(6) are equivalent to: \begin{enumerate} \item[(7)] $C$ is not positively hiding; \item[(8)] $C$ is not infinitely hiding. \end{enumerate} It suffices to check that $(4)\Rightarrow(7)\Rightarrow(8)\Rightarrow (2)$. In fact, the first two implications $(4)\Rightarrow(7)\Rightarrow(8)$ are trivial, while $(8)\Rightarrow(2)$ follows from Lemmas~\ref{l5.3} and \ref{l5.8}.
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications (1)=>(2)=>(3)=>(5)=>(6)=>(4)=>(2)=>(3)=>(1) assembled from the lemmas of Sections 2-6, plus (4)=>(7)=>(8)=>(2) in finite dimensions.

nodes.name: Point outside the closure
nodes.statement: Since $v\notin V_{\bar C}$, there is a real number $t_0>0$ such that $c_0+t_0v\notin \bar C$.
nodes.statement_short: Find t_0 with c_0+t_0v outside the closure of C.

nodes.name: Distance function f
nodes.statement: Consider the continuous function $$f:\bar{\mathbb R}_+\to\bar{\mathbb R}_+,\;\;f:t\mapsto \mathsf{dist}(c_0+tv,C),$$and observe that $f(0)=0$ as $c_0\in C$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce f(t)=dist(c_0+tv,C) with f(0)=0.

nodes.name: f tends to infinity
nodes.statement: We claim that $\lim_{t\to+\infty}f(t)=+\infty$. Since $c_0+t_0v\notin \bar C$, we can apply Hahn-Banach Theorem and find a linear functional $x^*\in X^*$ with unit norm such that $x^*(c_0+t_0v)>\sup x^*(\bar C)\ge x^*(c_0)$, which implies that $x^*(v)>0$. Then for any real number $t>t_0$ we get $$\mathsf{dist}(t v,C)=\inf_{c\in C}\|c_0+tv-c\|\ge \inf_{c\in C} |x^*(tv)-x^*(c-c_0)|=t x^*(v)-\sup x^*(C-c_0)$$ and hence $\lim_{t\to+\infty}\mathsf{dist}(c_0+tv,C)=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim that f(t) tends to infinity.

nodes.name: Hahn-Banach separation
nodes.statement: Since $c_0+t_0v\notin \bar C$, we can apply Hahn-Banach Theorem and find a linear functional $x^*\in X^*$ with unit norm such that $x^*(c_0+t_0v)>\sup x^*(\bar C)\ge x^*(c_0)$, which implies that $x^*(v)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Separate by Hahn-Banach to get x^*(v)>0.

nodes.name: Linear lower bound
nodes.statement: Then for any real number $t>t_0$ we get $$\mathsf{dist}(t v,C)=\inf_{c\in C}\|c_0+tv-c\|\ge \inf_{c\in C} |x^*(tv)-x^*(c-c_0)|=t x^*(v)-\sup x^*(C-c_0)$$ and hence $\lim_{t\to+\infty}\mathsf{dist}(c_0+tv,C)=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the distance below by t x^*(v) minus a constant.

nodes.name: Intermediate value
nodes.statement: By the continuity of $f$, there is a positive real number $t$ with $\mathsf{dist}(c_0+tv,C)=f(t)=\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by continuity of f.

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: We lose no generality assuming that $0\in A\cap B$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG 0 lies in both sets.

nodes.name: Distinguishing direction
nodes.statement: If $V_A\ne V_B$, then we can find a vector $v\in X$ that lies in $V_A\setminus V_B$ or in $V_B\setminus V_A$. We lose no generality assuming that $v\in V_B\setminus V_A$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the cones differ and pick v in V_B minus V_A.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l2.3}, there is a positive real number $t$ such that $\mathsf{dist}(tv,A)>\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,B)$, which is not possible as $tv\in V_B\subset B$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.3 gives tv in B far from A, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: We lose no generality assuming that $0\in C$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG 0 is in C.

nodes.name: Weak* closedness
nodes.statement: Observe that the dual characteristic cone $$V^*_{V_C}=\{x^*\in X^*:\sup x^*(V_C)<\infty\}=\{x^*\in X^*:\sup x^*(V_C)=0\}=\bigcap_{v\in V_C}\{x^*\in X^*:x^*(v)\le 0\}$$is weak$^*$ closed in $X^*$, being an intersection of weak$^*$-closed half-spaces in $X^*$.
nodes.statement_short: V*_{V_C} is an intersection of weak*-closed half-spaces.

nodes.name: First inclusion
nodes.statement: So, the inclusion $V^*_C\subset V^*_{V_C}$ implies $\mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)\subset V^*_{V_C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Obtain the inclusion of the weak* closure.

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the reverse inclusion $V^*_{V_C}\subset \mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the reverse inclusion.

nodes.name: Counter-functional
nodes.statement: Assume conversely that it is not true and find a functional $x^*\in V^*_{V_C}\setminus\mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a functional in V*_{V_C} outside the closure.

nodes.name: Weak* separation
nodes.statement: By the Hahn-Banach Theorem applied to the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$, there is an element $x\in X$ that separates $x^*$ from $\mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)$ in the sense that $$x^*(x)>\sup\{v^*(x):v^*\in\mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)\}\ge\sup\{v^*(x):v^*\in V^*_C\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Separate it by an element x of X.

nodes.name: x is non-positive on V*_C
nodes.statement: We claim that $v^*(x)\le 0$ for all functionals $v^*\in V^*_C$. Assuming that $v^*(x)>0$, we can find a positive real number $\lambda$ so large that $\lambda v^*(x)>x^*(x)$, which contradicts the choice of $x$ (because $\lambda v^*\in V^*_C$). So, $v^*(x)\le 0$ for all $v^*\in V^*_C$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim v^*(x)<=0 for all v^* in V*_C.

nodes.name: Scaling argument
nodes.statement: Assuming that $v^*(x)>0$, we can find a positive real number $\lambda$ so large that $\lambda v^*(x)>x^*(x)$, which contradicts the choice of $x$ (because $\lambda v^*\in V^*_C$).
nodes.statement_short: Scaling v^* would contradict the choice of x.

nodes.name: Sign established
nodes.statement: So, $v^*(x)\le 0$ for all $v^*\in V^*_C$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence v^*(x)<=0.

nodes.name: x in the characteristic cone
nodes.statement: We claim that $x\in V_C$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim x lies in V_C.

nodes.name: Ray leaves C
nodes.statement: In the opposite case, we could find a positive real number $t>0$ such that $tx\notin C$ (here we recall that $0\in C$).
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise some tx is outside C.

nodes.name: Separate tx
nodes.statement: Applying Hahn-Banach Theorem, find a linear functional $v^*\in X^*$ such that $v^*(tx)>\sup v^*(C)\ge 0$. Then $v^*\in V^*_C$ and $v^*(x)>0$, which contradicts the property of $x$ established at the end of the preceding paragraph.
nodes.statement_short: Hahn-Banach yields v^* in V*_C with v^*(x)>0, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This contradiction shows that $x\in V_C$ and then $x^*(x)>0$ implies that $\sup x^*(V_C)=\infty$, which contradicts the choice of the functional $x^*\in V^*_{V_C}$. This contradiction completes the proof of the inclusion $V^*_{V_C}\subset \mathrm{cl}^*(V^*_C)$.
nodes.statement_short: x in V_C forces sup x^*(V_C)=infinity, contradiction.

nodes.name: Lattice structure
nodes.statement: We consider the space $\mathbb R^n$ as a Banach lattice with coordinatewise operations of minimum and maximum. \smallskip
nodes.statement_short: View R^n as a Banach lattice.

nodes.name: Part 1
nodes.statement: 1. The first statement is easy and is left to the reader as an exercise. \smallskip
nodes.statement_short: Part 1 is left to the reader.

nodes.name: Part 2
nodes.statement: 2. To prove the second statement, we first check that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 1})<\infty$. By Lemma~\ref{l2.1}(2), $P_{\mathbf 1}=\mathrm{conv}(F)+\mathrm{cone}(E)$ for some finite sets $F,E\subset X$. It follows that the cone $\mathrm{cone}(E)$ coincides with the characteristic cone $P_{\mathbf 0}$ of $P_{\mathbf 1}$ and hence $P_{\mathbf 1}=\mathrm{conv}(F)+P_{\mathbf 0}$. Then $$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\mathrm{conv}(F)+P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\mathrm{conv}(F),\{0\})<\infty.$$ Let $a=\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}a_i$. Taking into account that that the norm of the Banach space $X$ is homogeneous and that $P_{\mathbf 0}\subset P_{\mathbf a}\subset P_{a\mathbf 1}$, we get the required inequality $$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf a},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{a\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})=a\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})\cdot \max_{1\le i\le n}a_i<\infty.$$
nodes.statement_short: Prove the distance bound.

nodes.name: Finite distance first
nodes.statement: 2. To prove the second statement, we first check that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 1})<\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: First check d_H(P_0,P_1) is finite.

nodes.name: Minkowski-Weyl decomposition
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l2.1}(2), $P_{\mathbf 1}=\mathrm{conv}(F)+\mathrm{cone}(E)$ for some finite sets $F,E\subset X$.
nodes.statement_short: Write P_1=conv(F)+cone(E) by Lemma 2.1(2).

nodes.name: Finite distance
nodes.statement: It follows that the cone $\mathrm{cone}(E)$ coincides with the characteristic cone $P_{\mathbf 0}$ of $P_{\mathbf 1}$ and hence $P_{\mathbf 1}=\mathrm{conv}(F)+P_{\mathbf 0}$. Then $$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\mathrm{conv}(F)+P_{\mathbf 0},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\mathrm{conv}(F),\{0\})<\infty.$$
nodes.statement_short: cone(E)=P_0, so d_H(P_1,P_0) is at most d_H(conv F,{0}).

nodes.name: Homogeneity
nodes.statement: Let $a=\max\limits_{1\le i\le n}a_i$. Taking into account that that the norm of the Banach space $X$ is homogeneous and that $P_{\mathbf 0}\subset P_{\mathbf a}\subset P_{a\mathbf 1}$, we get the required inequality $$\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf a},P_{\mathbf 0})\le\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{a\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})=a\cdot\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P_{\mathbf 1},P_{\mathbf 0})\cdot \max_{1\le i\le n}a_i<\infty.$$
nodes.statement_short: Use P_0 within P_a within P_{a1} and homogeneity.

nodes.name: Trivial case and normalization
nodes.statement: The case $C=X$ is trivial because in this case the component $\mathcal H_C=\{X\}$ contains a unique convex set $X$, which is polyhedral as the intersection of the empty family of closed half-spaces. So, we assume that $\mathcal H_C$ contains some polyhedral convex set $P\ne X$. Without loss of generality we can assume that $0\in P$.
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of C=X; assume P is not X and contains 0.

nodes.name: Equal cones
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l2.4n}, $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)<\infty$ implies $V_C=V_P\ne X$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.4 gives V_C=V_P.

nodes.name: Half-space representation
nodes.statement: Write $P$ as a finite intersection of closed half-spaces $$P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big)$$ where $f_1,\dots,f_k:X\to\mathbb R$ are linear continuous functionals with unit norm and $a_1,\dots,a_k$ are some real numbers. It follows from $0\in P$ that $a_1,\dots,a_n\ge 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Write P as an intersection of half-spaces with a_i>=0.

nodes.name: Reduce to a cone
nodes.statement: According to Lemma~\ref{l2.6}, we lose no generality assuming that $a_1=\dots=a_k=0$, which implies that $P$ is a polyhedral cone that coincides with its characteristic cone $V_P=V_C$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2.6 assume P is the polyhedral cone V_C.

nodes.name: Finite generation
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l2.1}, $P=\mathrm{cone}(B)$ for some finite subset $B\subset X$.
nodes.statement_short: P=cone(B) for a finite B by Lemma 2.1.

nodes.name: Countable dense set
nodes.statement: By our assumption, the Banach space $X$ is finite-dimensional and hence separable. So, we can fix a countable dense subset $D\subset X$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a countable dense D in X.

nodes.name: Candidate sets C_F
nodes.statement: Next, for every finite subset $F\subset D$ consider its convex hull $\mathrm{conv}(F)$ and the polyhedral convex set $$C_F=\mathrm{conv}(F)+V_C=\mathrm{conv}(F)+\mathrm{cone}(B).$$
nodes.statement_short: Define C_F=conv(F)+cone(B).

nodes.name: Reduce to density
nodes.statement: It remains to check that the countable family $$\mathcal C=\{C_F:\mbox{$F$ is a finite subset of $D$}\}$$ is dense in $\mathcal H_C$.
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show these are dense in H_C.

nodes.name: Target set and ball
nodes.statement: Given a convex set $A\in\mathcal H$ and $\varepsilon>0$, we shall find a finite subset $F\subset D$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_F,A)< 2\varepsilon$. Denote by $\bar {\mathbb B}=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$ the closed unit ball of the Banach space $X$. Then for every $r>0$ the set $r\bar{\mathbb B}=\{r\cdot x:x\in\bar{\mathbb B}\}$ coincides with the closed $r$-ball $\{x\in X:\|x\|\le r\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix A and eps; introduce the closed unit ball.

Then for each $r\in\mathbb R_+$ we get the inclusion $$A_r=(A\cap r ar{\mathbb B})+P\subset A+P=A+V_A=A.$$ Assuming that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A_r,A)>\varepsilon$ for all $r\in\mathbb R_+$, we can construct an increasing sequence of positive real numbers $(r_n)_{n\in\omega}$ and a sequence of points $(x_n)_{n\in\omega}$ in $A$ such that $\|x_n\|\le r_n$ and $\mathsf{dist}(x_{n+1},A_{r_{n}})>\varepsilon$ for all $n\in\omega$.
