The Ramsey Theorem 5 of \cite{Ramsey} yields an infinite subset $\Omega\subset \omega$ and a number $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $i(n,m)=i$ and hence $f_i(x_m)>f_i(x_n)+\delta$ for all numbers $n<m$ in $\Omega$. This implies $\sup_{c\in C}f_i(c)\ge\sup_{n\in \Omega}f_i(x_n)=\infty$, which is not possible as $\sup f_i(C)\le (\sup f_i(P))+\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)<\infty$. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Truncation claim and its proof.

nodes.name: Apply Claim 3.2
nodes.statement: Claim~\ref{cl3.2} yields us a real number $r\in\mathbb R_+$ such that the intersection $A\cap r\bar{\mathbb B}$ is not empty and $\mathsf{dist}(A_r,A)<\varepsilon$ where $A_r=(A\cap r\bar{\mathbb B})+P$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose r with A_r eps-close to A.

nodes.name: Polytope approximation
nodes.statement: By \cite{Gruber}, the compact convex set $A\cap r\bar{\mathbb B}$ can be approximated by a finite subset $F\subset D$ such that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\mathrm{conv}(F),A\cap r\bar {\mathbb B})<\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate the compact part by conv(F), F in D.

nodes.name: Triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Then the polyhedral convex set $C_F=\mathrm{conv}(F)+P$ lies on Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_F,A_r)<\varepsilon$ from the set $A_r$ and hence on Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_F,A)\le \mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_F,A_r)+\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A_r,A)<2\varepsilon$ from $A$.
nodes.statement_short: C_F is within 2 eps of A.

nodes.name: A_r lies in A
nodes.statement: It follows from $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A,C)<\infty$ that $V_A=V_C=P$, see Lemma~\ref{l2.4n}. Then for each $r\in\mathbb R_+$ we get the inclusion $$A_r=(A\cap r\bar{\mathbb B})+P\subset A+P=A+V_A=A.$$
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2.4 V_A=P, so A_r is a subset of A.

nodes.name: Escaping sequence
nodes.statement: Assuming that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(A_r,A)>\varepsilon$ for all $r\in\mathbb R_+$, we can construct an increasing sequence of positive real numbers $(r_n)_{n\in\omega}$ and a sequence of points $(x_n)_{n\in\omega}$ in $A$ such that $\|x_n\|\le r_n$ and $\mathsf{dist}(x_{n+1},A_{r_{n}})>\varepsilon$ for all $n\in\omega$. Consequently, for every $n<m$ we get $$(x_m+\varepsilon\bar{\mathbb B})\cap(x_n+P)\subset (x_m+\varepsilon\bar{\mathbb B})\cap (A_{r_n}+P)=\emptyset,$$ which implies $x_m-x_n\notin\varepsilon\bar{\mathbb B}+P$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume otherwise and build x_n with x_m-x_n outside eps B+P.

nodes.name: Choose delta
nodes.statement: Let us recall that $P=\bigcap_{i=1}^k H_i$ where $H_i=f_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big)$ for $i\le k$. Using Lemma~\ref{l2.6}, we can choose $\delta>0$ such that $\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,\delta]\big)\subset P+\varepsilon\mathbb B$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.6 gives delta with the delta-relaxed cone inside P+eps B.

nodes.name: Violated facet
nodes.statement: It follows that for any $n<m$ we get $x_m-x_n\notin \bigcap_{i=1}^nf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,\delta]\big)$ and hence there is a number $i=i(n,m)\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $x_m-x_n\notin f_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,\delta]\big)$ and hence $f_i(x_m)>f_i(x_n)+\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Each pair n<m violates some facet f_i by delta.

nodes.name: Colouring
nodes.statement: The correspondence $i:(n,m)\to i(n,m)$ can be thought as a finite coloring of the set $[\omega]^2=\{(n,m)\in\omega^2:n<m\}$ of pairs of positive integers.
nodes.statement_short: View i(n,m) as a finite colouring of pairs.

nodes.name: Ramsey's theorem
nodes.statement: The Ramsey Theorem 5 of \cite{Ramsey} yields an infinite subset $\Omega\subset \omega$ and a number $i\in\{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $i(n,m)=i$ and hence $f_i(x_m)>f_i(x_n)+\delta$ for all numbers $n<m$ in $\Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Ramsey gives an infinite monochromatic set.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: This implies $\sup_{c\in C}f_i(c)\ge\sup_{n\in \Omega}f_i(x_n)=\infty$, which is not possible as $\sup f_i(C)\le (\sup f_i(P))+\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)<\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: f_i would be unbounded on C, contradicting finite distance.

nodes.name: Trivial case
nodes.statement: The statement of the lemma is trivial if $C=X$. So, we assume that $C\ne X$ and $\mathcal H_C$ contains a polyhedral convex set $P$.
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of C=X.

nodes.name: Half-space representation
nodes.statement: Replacing $P$ by its shift, we can assume that $0\in P$. Write $P$ as a finite intersection of closed half-spaces $$P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big),$$ where $f_1,\dots,f_k:X\to\mathbb R$ are suitable linear continuous functionals and $a_1,\dots,a_k$ are suitable non-negative real numbers.
nodes.statement_short: Assume 0 in P and write P via functionals f_i.

nodes.name: Polyhedral cone, lineality space
nodes.statement: It follows from $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)<\infty$ that the characteristic cone $$V_C=V_P=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big)$$ is polyhedral and the closed linear subspace $$Z=-V_C\cap V_C=\bigcap_{i=1}^kf_i^{-1}(0)$$has finite codimension in $X$.
nodes.statement_short: V_C=V_P is polyhedral and Z has finite codimension.

nodes.name: Pass to the quotient
nodes.statement: Then the quotient Banach space $Y=X/Z$ is finite-dimensional. Taking into account that $Z\subset V_P\cap V_C$ and applying Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(1,3), we conclude that the images $qC$ and $qP$ are closed convex sets in $Y$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(qC,qP)<\infty$. Moreover, the convex set $qP$ is polyhedral in $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: In Y=X/Z the images are closed at finite distance (Lemma 3.3).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: Since the Banach space $Y$ is finite-dimensional, it is legal to apply Lemma~\ref{l3.1} in order to find a dense countable subset $\mathcal D_Y\in\mathcal H_{qC}$ that consists of polyhedral convex sets.
nodes.statement_short: Get a countable dense polyhedral family in H_{qC}.

nodes.name: Lift back
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(2), the countable family $\mathcal D_X=\{q^{-1}(D):D\in\mathcal D_X\}$ consists of polyhedral convex subsets of $X$ and by Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(3) is dense in the component $\mathcal H_C$ of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Preimages are polyhedral and dense in H_C.

nodes.name: Trivial case
nodes.statement: The lemma trivially holds if $x$ or $y$ belongs to the set $C$. So, we assume that $x,y\notin C$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume x,y are not in C.

nodes.name: Convex representations
nodes.statement: It follows that the point $x\in\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})\setminus C$ can be written as $x=t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x$ for some $t_x\in(0,1]$ and $c_x\in C$. The same is true for the point $y\in\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{b\})\setminus C$ which can be written as $y=t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y$ for some $t_y\in(0,1]$ and $c_y\in C$.
nodes.statement_short: Write x and y as convex combinations with points of C.

nodes.name: Meeting point
nodes.statement: By our assumption, the intersection $[a,b]\cap C$ contains some point $c=ta+(1-t)b$ where $t\in[0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Take c=ta+(1-t)b in C.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: The lemma will be proved as soon as we check that the segment $[x,y]$ meets the convex hull $\mathrm{conv}(\{c,c_x,c_y\})\subset C$ of the 3-element set $\{c,c_x,c_y\}\subset C$. This will follow as soon as we find real numbers $u,\alpha,\alpha_x,\alpha_y\in[0,1]$ such that $\alpha+\alpha_x+\alpha_y=1$ and $$\alpha c+\alpha_xc_x+\alpha_yc_y=ux+(1-u)y=u(t_xa+(1-t_x)c_x)+(1-u)(t_yb+(1-t_y)c_y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finding convex coefficients.

nodes.name: Solve for u
nodes.statement: The number $u\in[0,1]$ can be found from the equation $$ut_xa+(1-u)t_yb=(ut_x+(1-u)t_y)(ta+(1-t)b)=(ut_x+(1-u)t_y)c,$$ which has a well-defined solution $$u=\frac{t\cdot t_y}{t\cdot t_y+(1-t)t_x}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Solve for u explicitly.

nodes.name: Remaining coefficients
nodes.statement: The remaining numbers $\alpha,\alpha_x$ and $\alpha_y$ can be found as $$\alpha=ut_x+(1-u)t_y,\quad \alpha_x=u(1-t_x),\quad\alpha_y=(1-u)(1-t_y).$$
nodes.statement_short: Give alpha, alpha_x, alpha_y.

nodes.name: Reduce to C positively hiding
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal H_C=\mathcal H_P$, we lose no generality assuming that the convex set $C$ itself is positively hiding, which means that there is an infinite subset $A\subset X\setminus C$ on positive distance $\varepsilon=\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)$ from $C$, which is hidden behind the set $C$ in the sense that for any distinct points $a,b\in A$ the affine segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG C itself is positively hiding with hidden set A at distance eps.

nodes.name: Points b_a
nodes.statement: Fix any point $c_0\in C$ and for every point $a\in A$ choose a point $b_a\in[c_0,a]$ on the distance $\mathsf{dist}(b_a,C)=\varepsilon$ from $C$. The choice of the point $b_a$ is possible as $\mathsf{dist}(a,C)\ge\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose b_a on [c_0,a] at distance eps.

nodes.name: B is hidden
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{l4.1} guarantees that the set $B=\{b_a:a\in A\}$ is infinite and is hidden behind the set $C$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 4.1 B is infinite and hidden behind C.

nodes.name: B is near C
nodes.statement: Moreover, this set lies in the $2\varepsilon$-neighborhood $C+2\varepsilon\mathbb B$ of $C$. Here $\mathbb B=\{x\in X:\|x\|< 1\}$ stands for the open unit ball in the Banach space $X$.
nodes.statement_short: B lies in the 2 eps-neighbourhood.

nodes.name: Sets C_beta
nodes.statement: Now for any subset $\beta\subset B$ consider the convex set $C_\beta=\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\beta)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define C_beta=conv(C with beta).

nodes.name: C_beta closed
nodes.statement: Applying Lemma~\ref{l4.1} one can show that this set is closed in $X$ and $C_\beta=\bigcup_{b\in\beta}\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{b\})$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.1 shows C_beta is closed and a union of hulls.

nodes.name: C_beta in H_C
nodes.statement: Taking into account that $C\subset C_\beta\subset C+2\varepsilon\mathbb B$, we see that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,C_\beta)\le 2\varepsilon$ and hence $C_\beta$ belongs to the component $\mathcal H_C$ of $C$.
nodes.statement_short: C_beta is within 2 eps of C.

nodes.name: Separation of C_alpha and C_beta
nodes.statement: We claim that for any two distinct subsets $\alpha,\beta\subset B$, the convex sets $C_\alpha$ and $C_\beta$ lie on the Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\alpha,C_\beta)\ge\varepsilon$. Since $\alpha\ne\beta$, there is a point $b\in (\beta\setminus\alpha)\cup(\alpha\setminus\beta)$. We lose no generality assuming that $b\in\beta\setminus\alpha$. Then $b\in C_\beta$ and $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$. Indeed, assuming that $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)<\varepsilon$, we conclude that the open $\varepsilon$-ball $b+\varepsilon\mathbb B$ meets the set $C_\alpha=\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\alpha)=\bigcup_{a\in \alpha}\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})$ at some point $x$ that belongs to $\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})$ for some point $a\in\alpha$. Since the set $B\ni a,b$ is hidden behind the set $C$, the segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$. By Lemma~\ref{l4.1}, the segment $[x,b]$ also meets the set $C$, which is not possible as $[x,b]$ lies in the $\varepsilon$-ball $b+\varepsilon \mathbb B$, which does not meet $C$ as $\mathsf{dist}(b,C)=\varepsilon$. This contradiction shows that $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$ and hence $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\beta,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim distinct subsets give sets at distance at least eps.

nodes.name: Distinguishing point
nodes.statement: Since $\alpha\ne\beta$, there is a point $b\in (\beta\setminus\alpha)\cup(\alpha\setminus\beta)$. We lose no generality assuming that $b\in\beta\setminus\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick b in beta minus alpha.

nodes.name: Distance assertion
nodes.statement: Then $b\in C_\beta$ and $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Assert dist(b,C_alpha)>=eps.

nodes.name: Close point x
nodes.statement: Indeed, assuming that $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)<\varepsilon$, we conclude that the open $\varepsilon$-ball $b+\varepsilon\mathbb B$ meets the set $C_\alpha=\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\alpha)=\bigcup_{a\in \alpha}\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})$ at some point $x$ that belongs to $\mathrm{conv}(C\cup\{a\})$ for some point $a\in\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise some x in conv(C with a) is eps-close to b.

nodes.name: Hidden pair
nodes.statement: Since the set $B\ni a,b$ is hidden behind the set $C$, the segment $[a,b]$ meets the set $C$.
nodes.statement_short: [a,b] meets C.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l4.1}, the segment $[x,b]$ also meets the set $C$, which is not possible as $[x,b]$ lies in the $\varepsilon$-ball $b+\varepsilon \mathbb B$, which does not meet $C$ as $\mathsf{dist}(b,C)=\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: [x,b] meets C, impossible inside the eps-ball.

nodes.name: Distance at least eps
nodes.statement: This contradiction shows that $\mathsf{dist}(b,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$ and hence $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\beta,C_\alpha)\ge\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence d_H(C_beta,C_alpha)>=eps.

nodes.name: Cardinality count
nodes.statement: Now we see that the component $\mathcal H_C$ contains the subset $\mathcal C=\{C_\beta:\beta\subset B\}$ of cardinality $|\mathcal C|\ge 2^{|B|}\ge\mathfrak c$, consisting of points on mutual distance $\ge \varepsilon$. This implies that $\mathrm{dens}(\mathcal H_C)\ge |\mathcal C|\ge \mathfrak c$.
nodes.statement_short: 2^|B| eps-separated points give density at least c.

nodes.name: Hidden sequence
nodes.statement: Assume that the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ hides some infinite injectively enumerated set $\{a_n\}_{n\in\omega}\subset Z\setminus V_{\bar C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take an injectively enumerated hidden set a_n.

nodes.name: Rescale by Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l2.3}, for every $n\in\omega$, there is a real number $t_n>0$ such that $\mathsf{dist}(t_n a_n,C)>n$. It is clear that for the set $A=\{t_na_n\}_{n\in\omega}$ we get $\sup\limits_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\mathsf{dist}(t_na_n,C)=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose t_n with dist(t_n a_n,C)>n.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It remains to show that for every distinct numbers $n,m\in\omega$ the segment $[t_na_n,t_mb_m]$ intersects the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Remains: rescaled segments meet the cone.

nodes.name: Meeting point
nodes.statement: Since the set $\{a_n,a_m\}\subset A\subset Z$ is hidden behind $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$, the segment $[a_n,a_m]$ meets the cone $Z\cap V_{\bar C}$ at some point $c=\tau a_n+(1-\tau)a_m$ where $\tau\in[0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Take c in [a_n,a_m] in the cone.

nodes.name: Rescaled meeting point
nodes.statement: Then for the number $$u=\frac{\tau t_m}{\tau t_m+(1-\tau)t_n}\in[0,1]$$we get $$ ut_na_n+(1-u)t_ma_m=\frac{t_nt_n}{\tau t_m+(1-\tau)t_n}(\tau a_n+(1-\tau)a_m)=\frac{t_nt_m}{\tau t_m+(1-\tau)t_n}c\in [t_na_n,t_ma_m]\cap V_{\bar C} $$and hence the intersection $Z\cap V_{\bar C}\cap[t_na_n,t_ma_m]\ni ut_na_n+(1-u)t_ma_m$ is not empty.
nodes.statement_short: An explicit convex combination of t_na_n, t_ma_m is a positive multiple of c.

nodes.name: Inductive plan
nodes.statement: Let $\tilde A=\{\tilde a_n:n\in\omega\}$ be an injective enumeration of the countable set $\tilde A$. By induction, for every $n\in\omega$ we shall choose a point $a_n\in q^{-1}(\tilde a_n)\cap\mathrm{aff}(C)$ so that $[a_n,a_m]\cap C\ne\emptyset$ for every numbers $n<m$, and $a_n\in C$ if $\tilde a_n\in \tilde C$.
nodes.statement_short: Enumerate the hidden set and plan an inductive lift.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We start the inductive construction choosing any point $a_0\in q^{-1}(\tilde a_0)\cap\mathrm{aff}(C)$. Such point $a_0$ exists since $q(\mathrm{aff}(C))=\mathrm{aff}(\tilde C)$. If $\tilde a_0\in \tilde C$, then we can additionally assume that $a_0\in C$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a_0 in the preimage within aff(C).

Assume that for some $n\ge 1$ the points $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$ have been constructed. We need to choose a point $a_n\in q^{-1}(	ilde a_n)\cap\mathrm{aff}(C)$ so that $[a_i,a_n]\cap C

nodes.name: Easy case
nodes.statement: Assume that for some $n\ge 1$ the points $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$ have been constructed. We need to choose a point $a_n\in q^{-1}(\tilde a_n)\cap\mathrm{aff}(C)$ so that $[a_i,a_n]\cap C\ne\emptyset$ for all $i<n$. If $\tilde a_n\in\tilde C$, then let $a_n\in C$ be any point with $q(a_n)=\tilde a_n$. So, assume that $\tilde a_n\notin \tilde C$.
nodes.statement_short: If the image point lies in the image of C, lift inside C.

nodes.name: Lifted candidates
nodes.statement: Let $I_n=\{i\in \omega:i<n,\;\tilde a_i\notin\tilde C\}$. Since the set $\tilde A\subset\tilde X$ is hidden behind the convex set $\tilde C$, for every $i\in I_n$ the intersection $[\tilde a_i,\tilde a_n]\cap \tilde C$ contains some point $\tilde c_i$ which can be written as the convex combination $\tilde c_i=u_i\tilde a_i+(1-u_i)\tilde a_n$ for some $u_i\in(0,1)$. Since $\tilde c_i\in \tilde C$, there is a point $c_i\in C$ with $q(c_i)=\tilde c_i$. It follows from $\tilde a_n=\frac{\tilde c_i-u_i\tilde a_i}{1-u_i}$ that the point $a_i'=\frac{c_i-u_ia_i}{1-u_i}$ belongs to the preimage $q^{-1}(\tilde a_n)$.
nodes.statement_short: For each earlier i, lift the meeting point and get a candidate a_i'.

nodes.name: Common point
nodes.statement: It follows from $E=V_{E\cap C}-V_{E\cap C}$ that the intersection $\bigcap_{i\in I_n}(a_i'+V_{E\cap C})$ contains some point $a_n$. For this point we get $u_ia_i+(1-u_i)a_n\in c_i+V_{C}\subset C$ and hence $[a_i,a_n]\cap C\ne\emptyset$ for all $i<n$, which completes the inductive step.
nodes.statement_short: Since E is spanned by the cone, the translates intersect; take a_n there.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: After completing the inductive construction, we obtain the countable set $A=\{a_n\}_{n\in\omega}$ that has the required property.
nodes.statement_short: The lifted set A has the required property.

nodes.name: Hidden set downstairs
nodes.statement: If $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding, then $\tilde C_0$ hides some infinite set $\tilde A\subset \mathrm{aff}(\tilde C_0)$ such that $\sup_{\tilde a\in \tilde A}\mathsf{dist}(\tilde a,\tilde C)=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the hidden set in the quotient.

nodes.name: Lift by Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l5.4}, there is a set $A\subset \mathrm{aff}(C_0)$ with $q(A)=\tilde A$, hidden behind the set $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift it to a hidden set A upstairs.

nodes.name: Non-expansion
nodes.statement: Since the quotient operator $q:X\to \tilde X$ has norm $\|q\|\le 1$, for every point $a\in A$ and its image $\tilde a=q(a)$, we get $\mathsf{dist}(\tilde a,\tilde C)\le \mathsf{dist}(a,C)$.
nodes.statement_short: Quotient distances bound distances upstairs.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Consequently, $\sup_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)\ge \sup_{\tilde a\in \tilde A}\mathsf{dist}(\tilde a,\tilde C)=\infty$, which means that the set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding.
nodes.statement_short: Distances are unbounded, so C_0 is C-infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Unboundedness
nodes.statement: The equality $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that the open convex subset $C_0$ of the plane $Z$ is not bounded. Consequently, its characteristic cone $V_{C_0}=V_{\bar C_0}=Z\cap V_C$ is unbounded too.
nodes.statement_short: C_0 and its cone are unbounded.

nodes.name: Shape of the cone
nodes.statement: Moreover, the cone $V_{C_0}$ is not a plane, not a half-plane, and not a line (otherwise $C_0$ would be on finite Hausdorff distance from its characteristic cone $V_{C_0}$).
nodes.statement_short: The cone is not a plane, half-plane or line.

nodes.name: Basis e_1,e_2
nodes.statement: Consequently, we can choose two linearly independent vectors $e_1,e_2\in Z$ such that the cone $V_{C_0}$ is equal to $\mathrm{cone}(\{e_1\})$ or to $\mathrm{cone}(\{e_1,e_2\})$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose e_1,e_2 so the cone is cone{e_1} or cone{e_1,e_2}.

nodes.name: Coordinate functionals
nodes.statement: Let $e_1^*,e_2^*\in Z^*$ be the coordinate functionals corresponding to the base $e_1,e_2$ of $Z$. This means that $z=e_1^*(z)e_1+e_2^*(z)e_2$ for each vector $z\in Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce coordinate functionals.

nodes.name: Two-dimensional cone
nodes.statement: If $V_{C_0}=\mathrm{cone}(\{e_1,e_2\})$, then the equality $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that $\inf e_1^*(C_0)=-\infty$ or $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$. We lose no generality assuming that $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Case of a two-dimensional cone.

nodes.name: Ray cone
nodes.statement: If $V_{C_0}=\mathrm{cone}(\{e_1\})$, then the equality $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$ or $\sup e_2^*(C_0)=+\infty$. Changing $e_2$ to $-e_2$, if necessary, we can assume that $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Case of a ray.

nodes.name: Reunion
nodes.statement: So, in both cases we can assume that $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: In both cases inf e_2^*(C_0)=-infinity.

nodes.name: Inductive plan
nodes.statement: By induction, we shall construct a sequence of points $(a_n)_{n\in\omega}$ in $\mathrm{cone}(\{e_1,-e_2\})$ such that for every $n\in\omega$ the following conditions are satisfied: \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathsf{dist}(a_n,C)>n$; \item $e_1^*(a_{n})>e_1^*(a_{n-1})>0$, $e_2^*(a_n)<e_2^*(a_{n-1})<0$, and $\dfrac{|e_2^*(a_n)|}{e_1^*(a_n)}<\dfrac{|e_2^*(a_{n-1})|}{e_1^*(a_{n-1})}$; \item $[a_n,a_{k}]\cap C_0\ne\emptyset$ for all $k<n$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Plan an inductive sequence with conditions (1)-(3).

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We start the inductive construction selecting a point $a_0\in\mathbb R_+\cdot(e_1-e_2)$ on the distance $\mathsf{dist}(a_0,C)>0$ from the set $C$. Such point $a_0$ exists because $e_1-e_2\notin V_{C_0}=Z\cap V_C$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a_0 on R_+(e_1-e_2) outside C.

nodes.statement: Now assume that for some $n\in\mathbb N$ we have constructed points $a_0,\dots,a_n\in\mathrm{cone}(\{e_1,-e_2\})$ satisfying the conditions (1)--(3). It follows from $\inf e_2^*(C_0)=-\infty$ and $e_1\in V_{C_0}\setminus(-V_{C_0})$ that there exists a point $c\in C_0$ such that $$e^*_1(c)>c_1^*(a_n),\;\;e^*_2(c)<e^*_2(a_n)\mbox{ \ and \ }\frac{|e^*_2(c)|}{e^*_1(c)}<\frac{|e^*_2(a_n)|}{e^*_1(a_n)}.$$

nodes.name: Choose a_{n+1}
nodes.statement: Now consider the vector $v=c-a_n$ and observe that $v\notin V_{C_0}=V_{\bar C_0}$. Consequently, $c+\mathbb R_+v\not\subset \bar C_0$, which allows us to find a point $a_{n+1}\in c+\mathbb R_+ v$ with $\mathsf{dist}(a_{n+1},C)>n+1$ (using Lemma~\ref{l2.3}). It can be shown that the point $a_{n+1}$ satisfies the condition (2).
nodes.statement_short: Using Lemma 2.3 pick a_{n+1} on the ray from c far from C.

nodes.name: Consecutive segment
nodes.statement: Since the segment $[a_n,a_{n+1}]$ contains the point $c$, it meets the set $C\cap Z$.
nodes.statement_short: [a_n,a_{n+1}] meets C.

nodes.name: Earlier segments
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to earlier points; [a_k,a_n] meets C_0 at c'.

nodes.name: Plane geometry
nodes.statement: By an elementary plane geometry argument one can prove that the segment $[a_k,a_{n+1}]$ meets the triangle $\mathrm{conv}(\{0,c',c\})\subset C_0$ and hence meets the set $C_0$. This completes the inductive step.
nodes.statement_short: [a_k,a_{n+1}] meets the triangle conv{0,c',c}.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: After completing the inductive construction, we obtain the infinite set $A=\{a_n\}_{n\in\omega}$ with $\sup_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)=\infty$ which is hidden behind $C_0$. This means that the set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding.
nodes.statement_short: The set A witnesses C-infinite hiding.

nodes.name: Induction base
nodes.statement: This lemma will be proved by induction on the dimension $\dim(Z)$ of $Z$. The lemma is trivially true if $\dim(Z)\le 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on dim Z; trivial for dim<=1.

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: Assume that the lemma has been proved for all triples $(X,C,Z)$ with $\dim(Z)<n$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the lemma for dim<n.

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis
nodes.statement: Now we prove this lemma for $\dim(Z)=n$. Assuming that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$, we need to prove that the convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding. To derive a contradiction, assume that $C_0$ is not $C$-infinitely hiding.
nodes.statement_short: Assume C_0 is not C-infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Assuming that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$, we need to prove that the convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding.
nodes.statement_short: State what must be proved.

nodes.name: Contradiction assumption
nodes.statement: To derive a contradiction, assume that $C_0$ is not $C$-infinitely hiding.
nodes.statement_short: Assume C_0 is not C-infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Claim 5.8
nodes.statement: In this case Lemma~\ref{l5.6} implies the following fact, which will be used several times in the subsequent proof. \begin{claim} For each two-dimensional linear subspace $Z_2\subset Z$ we get $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(Z_2\cap C_0,V_{Z_2\cap C_0})<\infty$. \end{claim}
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5.8 from Lemma 5.6.

nodes.name: Claim 5.9 with proof
nodes.statement: Now consider the characteristic cone $V_{C_0}=V_{\bar C_0}$ of the open convex set $C_0$ in $Z$. \begin{claim} The linear subspace $-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is trivial. \end{claim} \begin{proof} Assume that the linear subspace $E=-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is not equal to $\{0\}$. Consider the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/E$, the quotient operator $q:X\to \tilde X$, the convex set $\tilde C=q(C)$, and the finite-dimensional subspace $\tilde Z=q(Z)$ of dimension $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. Since the quotient operator $q|Z:Z\to\tilde Z$ is open, the convex set $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ is open in $\tilde Z$ and hence the convex set $\tilde Z\cap\tilde C$ has non-empty interior in $\tilde Z$. Since $E\subset V_C$, the set $\tilde C$ is closed in the Banach space $\tilde X$ by Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(1). Now we can see that the triple $(\tilde X,\tilde C,\tilde Z)$ satisfies the requirements of Lemma~\ref{l5.7} with $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. So, by the inductive assumption, the convex set $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding. Since $E=V_{E\cap C_0}=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$, we can apply Lemma~\ref{l5.4} to conclude that the open convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding in $X$. But this contradicts our assumption. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: The cone is pointed.

nodes.name: Claim 5.10 with proof
nodes.statement: \begin{claim} $\dim(V_{C_0})\ge 2$. \end{claim} \begin{proof} Assume conversely that $\dim(V_{C_0})\le 1$. The equality $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that the open convex subset $C_0$ is unbounded in the finite-dimensional linear space $Z\cap C_0$ and consequently $V_{C_0}\ne 0$. Since $-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}=\{0\}$, we conclude that $V_{C_0}=\bar{\mathbb R}_+ e$ for some non-zero vector $e\in V_{C_0}$. Now consider the linear subspace $E=\mathbb R e\subset Z$, the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/E$, the finite-dimensional linear subspace $\tilde Z=q(Z)$, the convex sets $\tilde C=q(C)$, and the open convex set $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$, which is dense in $\tilde C$. Claim~\ref{cl5.8} guarantees that the set $\tilde C_0$ has trivial characteristic cone and hence is bounded in the finite-dimensional space $\tilde Z$. This implies that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})<\infty$, which is a desired contradiction. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: The cone has dimension at least 2.

nodes.name: Polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: Since $C_0$ is not $C$-infinitely hiding, Lemma~\ref{l5.2}, guarantees that the characteristic cone $V_{C_0}$ is polyhedral in $Z$ and hence it can be written as a finite intersection of closed half-spaces $$V_{C_0}=\bigcap_{i=1}^k f_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big)$$determined by some linear functionals $f_1,\dots,f_k:Z\to\mathbb R$. We shall assume that the number $k$ in this representation is the smallest possible.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.2 makes V_{C_0} polyhedral; take a minimal representation.

nodes.name: Unbounded functional
nodes.statement: It follows from $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ and Lemma~\ref{l2.6} that $\sup f_i(C_0)=\infty$ for some $i\le k$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 2.6 some f_i is unbounded on C_0.

nodes.name: Quotient by e
nodes.statement: Claim~\ref{cl5.11} yields a non-zero vector $e\in f_i^{-1}(0)\cap V_{C_0}$. Consider the 1-dimensional linear subspace $E=\mathbb R e$ of $X$ and let $\tilde X=X/E$ be the quotient Banach space. Observe that $\tilde X$ contains the finite-dimensional linear subspace $\tilde Z=Z/E$ of dimension $\dim(\tilde Z)=\dim(Z)-1<n$. Let $q:X\to\tilde X$ be the quotient operator, and $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$, $\tilde C=q(C)$ be the images of the convex sets $C_0$ and $C$ in $\tilde X$. It follows from $E=q^{-1}(0)\subset Z$ that $\tilde Z\cap\tilde C=q(Z\cap C)$ and $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ coincides with the interior of the set $q(Z\cap C)=\tilde Z\cap\tilde C$ in $\tilde Z$. So, the triple $(\tilde X,\tilde Z,\tilde C)$ satisfies the assumptions of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Quotient by the line through e; the triple satisfies the hypotheses.

nodes.name: Quotient section far from its cone
nodes.statement: We claim that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C_0,V_{\tilde C_0})=\infty$. Since $E\subset f_i^{-1}(0)$, there is a linear functional $\tilde f_i:\tilde Z\to \mathbb R$ such that $f_i=\tilde f_i\circ q|Z$. \begin{claim} $V_{\tilde C_0}\subset \tilde f_i^{-1}(-\infty,0]$. \end{claim} \begin{proof} Assume conversely that the characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}$ contains some vector $w\in \tilde Z$ with $\tilde f_i(w)>0$. Then $\mathbb R_+w\subset \tilde Z$. Pick any vector $v\in q^{-1}(w)\subset Z$ and consider the two-dimensional subspace $Z_2=\mathrm{lin}(\{v,e\})$ spanning the vectors $v$ and $e$. Observe that for every $t\in\mathbb R$ we get $f_i(v+te)=\tilde f_i(w)>0$, which implies that $(v+t\mathbb R)\cap V_{Z_2\cap C}=\emptyset$. Then $V_{Z_2\cap C}\subset \mathbb R e-\bar{\mathbb R}_+v$ and $q(V_{Z_2\cap C})\subset -\bar{\mathbb R}_+w$. On the other hand, the projection $q(Z_2\cap C)$ contains the half-line $\mathbb R_+ w$, which implies that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(Z_2\cap C,V_{Z_2\cap C})=\infty$. But this contradicts Claim~\ref{cl5.8}. \end{proof} Taking into account that $\infty=\sup f_i(C_0)=\sup \tilde f_i(\tilde C_0)$, we conclude that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C_0,V_{\tilde C_0})=\infty$ and by the inductive assumption, the open convex set $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding (as $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$).
nodes.statement_short: Claim the quotient section is at infinite distance from its cone.

nodes.name: Induced functional
nodes.statement: Since $E\subset f_i^{-1}(0)$, there is a linear functional $\tilde f_i:\tilde Z\to \mathbb R$ such that $f_i=\tilde f_i\circ q|Z$.
nodes.statement_short: f_i factors through q.

nodes.name: Claim 5.12 with proof
nodes.statement: \begin{claim} $V_{\tilde C_0}\subset \tilde f_i^{-1}(-\infty,0]$. \end{claim} \begin{proof} Assume conversely that the characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}$ contains some vector $w\in \tilde Z$ with $\tilde f_i(w)>0$. Then $\mathbb R_+w\subset \tilde Z$. Pick any vector $v\in q^{-1}(w)\subset Z$ and consider the two-dimensional subspace $Z_2=\mathrm{lin}(\{v,e\})$ spanning the vectors $v$ and $e$. Observe that for every $t\in\mathbb R$ we get $f_i(v+te)=\tilde f_i(w)>0$, which implies that $(v+t\mathbb R)\cap V_{Z_2\cap C}=\emptyset$. Then $V_{Z_2\cap C}\subset \mathbb R e-\bar{\mathbb R}_+v$ and $q(V_{Z_2\cap C})\subset -\bar{\mathbb R}_+w$. On the other hand, the projection $q(Z_2\cap C)$ contains the half-line $\mathbb R_+ w$, which implies that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(Z_2\cap C,V_{Z_2\cap C})=\infty$. But this contradicts Claim~\ref{cl5.8}. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: The quotient cone lies in a half-space.

nodes.name: Apply induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: Taking into account that $\infty=\sup f_i(C_0)=\sup \tilde f_i(\tilde C_0)$, we conclude that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C_0,V_{\tilde C_0})=\infty$ and by the inductive assumption, the open convex set $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding (as $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$).
nodes.statement_short: Infinite distance holds, so the induction hypothesis applies.

nodes.name: Lift by Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: Since $E=\mathbb R_+e-\mathbb R_+e=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$, we can apply Lemma~\ref{l5.4} to conclude that the open convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding in $X$. This contradiction completes the proof of Lemma~\ref{l5.7}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.4 lifts the hiding, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Non-trivial lineality
nodes.statement: Assume that the linear subspace $E=-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}$ is not equal to $\{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the lineality space E is non-zero.

nodes.name: Quotient with open image
nodes.statement: Consider the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/E$, the quotient operator $q:X\to \tilde X$, the convex set $\tilde C=q(C)$, and the finite-dimensional subspace $\tilde Z=q(Z)$ of dimension $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. Since the quotient operator $q|Z:Z\to\tilde Z$ is open, the convex set $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ is open in $\tilde Z$ and hence the convex set $\tilde Z\cap\tilde C$ has non-empty interior in $\tilde Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to X/E; the image of C_0 is open in the quotient section.

nodes.name: Closed image
nodes.statement: Since $E\subset V_C$, the set $\tilde C$ is closed in the Banach space $\tilde X$ by Lemma~\ref{l3.3}(1).
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.3(1) gives closedness.

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: Now we can see that the triple $(\tilde X,\tilde C,\tilde Z)$ satisfies the requirements of Lemma~\ref{l5.7} with $\dim(\tilde Z)<\dim(Z)=n$. So, by the inductive assumption, the convex set $\tilde C_0$ is $\tilde C$-infinitely hiding.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the induction hypothesis in lower dimension.

nodes.name: Lift and contradict
nodes.statement: Since $E=V_{E\cap C_0}=V_{E\cap C_0}-V_{E\cap C_0}$, we can apply Lemma~\ref{l5.4} to conclude that the open convex set $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding in $X$. But this contradicts our assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.4 lifts the hiding, contradicting the assumption.

nodes.name: Assume small cone
nodes.statement: Assume conversely that $\dim(V_{C_0})\le 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume dim V_{C_0}<=1.

nodes.name: Non-zero cone
nodes.statement: The equality $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\infty$ implies that the open convex subset $C_0$ is unbounded in the finite-dimensional linear space $Z\cap C_0$ and consequently $V_{C_0}\ne 0$.
nodes.statement_short: C_0 is unbounded so the cone is non-zero.

nodes.name: Ray
nodes.statement: Since $-V_{C_0}\cap V_{C_0}=\{0\}$, we conclude that $V_{C_0}=\bar{\mathbb R}_+ e$ for some non-zero vector $e\in V_{C_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: The cone is a ray R_+e.

nodes.name: Quotient by the ray
nodes.statement: Now consider the linear subspace $E=\mathbb R e\subset Z$, the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/E$, the finite-dimensional linear subspace $\tilde Z=q(Z)$, the convex sets $\tilde C=q(C)$, and the open convex set $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$, which is dense in $\tilde C$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the quotient by Re.

nodes.name: Bounded image
nodes.statement: Claim~\ref{cl5.8} guarantees that the set $\tilde C_0$ has trivial characteristic cone and hence is bounded in the finite-dimensional space $\tilde Z$. This implies that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})<\infty$, which is a desired contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5.8 makes the image bounded, contradiction.

nodes.name: Point x
nodes.statement: By the minimality of $k$ the cone $V=\bigcap\{f^{-1}_j\big((-\infty,0]\big):1\le j\le k,\;\;j\ne i\}$ is strictly larger than $V_{C_0}$ and hence contains a point $x\in V\setminus V_{C_0}$. For this point $x$ we get $f_j(x)\le 0$ for all $j\ne i$, and $f_i(x)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives x violating only f_i.

nodes.name: Point y
nodes.statement: Since $\dim(V_{C_0})\ge 2$, there exists a vector $y\in V_{C_0}\setminus\mathbb R x$. Such choice of $x$ guarantees that $0\notin [x,y]$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick y in the cone off the line Rx.

nodes.name: Zero of f_i
nodes.statement: Since $f_i(y)\le 0$ and $f_i(x)>0$, there is a point $e\in [x,y]$ with $f_i(e)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Find e in [x,y] with f_i(e)=0.

nodes.name: e lies in the facet
nodes.statement: For every $j\ne i$, the inequalities $f_j(x)\le 0$ and $f_j(y)\le 0$ imply $f_j(e)\le 0$. Conseqeuntly, $e$ is a required non-zero vector in $f_i^{-1}(0)\cap V_{C_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: e satisfies the other inequalities.

nodes.name: Bad direction
nodes.statement: Assume conversely that the characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}$ contains some vector $w\in \tilde Z$ with $\tilde f_i(w)>0$. Then $\mathbb R_+w\subset \tilde Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume w in the cone with positive f_i.

nodes.name: Plane Z_2
nodes.statement: Pick any vector $v\in q^{-1}(w)\subset Z$ and consider the two-dimensional subspace $Z_2=\mathrm{lin}(\{v,e\})$ spanning the vectors $v$ and $e$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift w to v and take Z_2=lin{v,e}.

nodes.name: Cone of the section
nodes.statement: Observe that for every $t\in\mathbb R$ we get $f_i(v+te)=\tilde f_i(w)>0$, which implies that $(v+t\mathbb R)\cap V_{Z_2\cap C}=\emptyset$. Then $V_{Z_2\cap C}\subset \mathbb R e-\bar{\mathbb R}_+v$ and $q(V_{Z_2\cap C})\subset -\bar{\mathbb R}_+w$.
nodes.statement_short: Locate the characteristic cone of the section Z_2 cap C.

nodes.name: Contradiction with Claim 5.8
nodes.statement: On the other hand, the projection $q(Z_2\cap C)$ contains the half-line $\mathbb R_+ w$, which implies that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(Z_2\cap C,V_{Z_2\cap C})=\infty$. But this contradicts Claim~\ref{cl5.8}.
nodes.statement_short: The section is at infinite distance from its cone, contradicting Claim 5.8.

nodes.name: Relative interior
nodes.statement: It is well-known that $C\cap A$ has non-empty interior $C_0$ in its affine hull $\mathrm{aff}(C\cap A)$. Moreover, $C\cap A$ coincides with the closure $\bar C_0$ of $C_0$ in $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall C cap A has non-empty relative interior C_0.

nodes.name: Linear section
nodes.statement: Shifting the set $C$, if necessary, we can assume that $0\in C_0$. Then $Z=\mathrm{aff}(C_0)$ is a finite-dimensional linear subspace of $X$ such that $C\cap Z=C\cap A$ has non-empty interior $C_0$ which contains zero and is dense in $C\cap Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Shift so that 0 is in C_0 and take Z=aff(C_0).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.7
nodes.statement: It follows that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_0,V_{C_0})=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(Z\cap C,V_{Z\cap C})=\infty$ and hence $C_0$ is $C$-infinitely hiding by Lemma~\ref{l5.7}, and $C$ is infinitely hiding as $C_0\subset C$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.7 gives C-infinite hiding, hence C is infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Non-empty interior
nodes.statement: Replacing $C$ by a shift of its closed neighborhood, we can assume that the convex subset $C$ of $X$ has non-empty interior $C_0$, which contains zero. After such replacement the cones $V_C$ and $V_C^*$ will not change, see Lemma~\ref{l2.4n}.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: WLOG C has interior containing 0; cones unchanged by Lemma 2.4.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: The biorthogonal sequence $\{(x_n,x_n^*)\}_{n\in\omega}$ will be constructed by induction. We start by choosing an arbitrary functional $x^*_0\in V^*_C$ and a point $x_0\in X$ with $1=\|x_0^*\|=x^*_0(x_0)\le \|x_0\|<4$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Start with x_0^* in V*_C and x_0.

nodes.name: Inductive data
nodes.statement: Assume that for some $k\in\omega$ a finite biorthogonal sequence $\{(x_n,x^*_n)\}_{n<k}\subset X\times V^*_C$ has been constructed so that $1=\|x^*_n\|\le\|x_n\|<4$ for all $n< k$. Let $L^*$ be the linear hull of the finite set $\{x^*_0,\dots,x^*_{k-1}\}$ in the dual Banach space $X^*$. In the compact set $L^*_2=\{x^*\in L:\|x^*\|\le 2\}$, choose a finite subset $F^*_2\subset L^*_2$ such that for each functional $x^*\in L^*_2$ there is a functional $y^*\in F^*_2$ with $\|x^*-y^*\|<\frac18$. For every functional $f\in F^*_2$ choose a point $x_f\in X$ such that $\|x_f\|=1$ and $f(x_f)>\|f\|-\frac18$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Given the first k pairs, take a finite 1/8-net of the 2-ball of their span and norming vectors x_f.

nodes.name: Quotient by E
nodes.statement: Let $E$ be the linear hull of the finite set $\{x_i:i<k\}\cup\{x_f:f\in F_2^*\}$ in $X$. Let $\tilde X=X/E$ be the quotient Banach space, $q:X\to\tilde X$ be the quotient operator, and $\tilde C=q(C)$ be the quotient image of the convex set $C$ in $\tilde X$. Since the quotient operator $q$ is open, the image $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ coincides with the interior of $\tilde C$ in $\tilde X$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Quotient by the span E of the x_i and x_f.

nodes.name: Trivial quotient cone
nodes.statement: We claim that the set $\tilde C_0$ has trivial characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}=\{0\}$. Assuming the converse, find a non-zero vector $\tilde v\in V_{\tilde C_0}$, choose any vector $v\in q^{-1}(\tilde v)$ and consider the finite-dimensional linear subspace $E_v=\mathrm{lin}(E\cup\{v\})$. The triviality of the characteristic cone $V_C=\{0\}$ implies that the intersection $E_v\cap C_0$ is bounded and then the image $q(E_v\cap C_0)=\mathbb R \tilde v\cap \tilde C_0$ also is bounded. So, $\bar{\mathbb R}_+\tilde v\not\subset C_0$, which contradicts $\tilde v\in V_{\tilde C_0}\setminus\{0\}$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Claim the quotient has trivial characteristic cone.

nodes.name: Non-zero direction
nodes.statement: Assuming the converse, find a non-zero vector $\tilde v\in V_{\tilde C_0}$, choose any vector $v\in q^{-1}(\tilde v)$ and consider the finite-dimensional linear subspace $E_v=\mathrm{lin}(E\cup\{v\})$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Assume a non-zero cone direction.

nodes.name: Bounded section
nodes.statement: The triviality of the characteristic cone $V_C=\{0\}$ implies that the intersection $E_v\cap C_0$ is bounded and then the image $q(E_v\cap C_0)=\mathbb R \tilde v\cap \tilde C_0$ also is bounded.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: The finite-dimensional section is bounded.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: So, $\bar{\mathbb R}_+\tilde v\not\subset C_0$, which contradicts $\tilde v\in V_{\tilde C_0}\setminus\{0\}$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction with the cone direction.

nodes.name: New functional
nodes.statement: The triviality of the cone $V_{\tilde C_0}=\{0\}$ implies that $\tilde C\ne \tilde X$, so we can find a functional $\tilde x_k^*\in V^*_{\tilde C_0}$ with unit norm $\|\tilde x_k^*\|=1$. Now consider the functional $x_k^*=\tilde x_k^*\circ q$ and observe that $\|x_k^*\|=\|\tilde x^*_k\|=1$ and $x_k^*(x_i)=0$ for all $i<k$ and $x_k^*(x_f)=0$ for all $f\in F_2^*$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Choose a unit functional x_k^* in V*_C vanishing on E.

nodes.name: Far from the span
nodes.statement: We claim that $\mathsf{dist}(x^*_k,L^*)>\frac14$. Assuming the converse, find a functional $l^*\in L^*$ with $\|x^*_k-l^*|\le \frac14$. Then $\|l^*\|\le\|x^*_k\|+\frac14$, so $l^*\in L_2^*$ and by the choice of the set $F_2^*$, we can find a functional $f\in F^*_2$ such that $\|l^*-f\|<\frac18$. Then $\|x^*_k-f\|\le\|x^*_k-l^*\|+\|l^*-f\|\le \frac14+\frac18=\frac38$, $\|f\|\ge\|x^*_k\|-\|x^*_k-f\|\ge 1-\frac38=\frac58$ and we obtain the contradiction: $$\frac48=\frac58-\frac18\le \|f\|-\frac18<f(x_f)=|x_k^*(x_f)-f(x_f)|\le\|x^*_k-f\|\cdot\|x_f\|\le\frac38.$$
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Claim x_k^* is at distance >1/4 from L^*.

nodes.name: Close functional
nodes.statement: Assuming the converse, find a functional $l^*\in L^*$ with $\|x^*_k-l^*|\le \frac14$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Assume l^* in L^* is 1/4-close.

nodes.name: Use the net
nodes.statement: Then $\|l^*\|\le\|x^*_k\|+\frac14$, so $l^*\in L_2^*$ and by the choice of the set $F_2^*$, we can find a functional $f\in F^*_2$ such that $\|l^*-f\|<\frac18$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Find f in the net close to l^*.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Then $\|x^*_k-f\|\le\|x^*_k-l^*\|+\|l^*-f\|\le \frac14+\frac18=\frac38$, $\|f\|\ge\|x^*_k\|-\|x^*_k-f\|\ge 1-\frac38=\frac58$ and we obtain the contradiction: $$\frac48=\frac58-\frac18\le \|f\|-\frac18<f(x_f)=|x_k^*(x_f)-f(x_f)|\le\|x^*_k-f\|\cdot\|x_f\|\le\frac38.$$
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Evaluating at x_f gives a contradiction.

nodes.name: Ball misses L^*
nodes.statement: This contradiction shows that $\mathsf{dist}(x^*_k,L^*)>\frac14$ and implies that the the closed $\frac14$-ball $B^*=\{x^*\in X^*:\|x^*-x^*_{k}\|\le \frac14\}$ centered at $x^*_{k}$ does not intersect $L^*$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: The 1/4-ball around x_k^* misses L^*.

nodes.name: Weak* compactness
nodes.statement: By the Banach-Alaoglu Theorem this ball is compact in the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Banach-Alaoglu: the ball is weak* compact.

nodes.name: Separation
nodes.statement: Now the Hahn-Banach Theorem applied to the weak$^*$ topology of $X^*$ yields us a point $x_{k}\in X$ that separates $L^*$ and $B^*$ in the sense that $\sup_{x^*\in L^*}x^*(x_{k})< \inf_{x^*\in B^*}x^*(x_{k})$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Separate L^* and the ball by x_k.

nodes.name: Biorthogonality
nodes.statement: It follows from the linearity of $L^*$ that $x^*(x_{k})=0$ for all $x^*\in L^*$. In particular, $x^*_i(x_{k})=0$ for all $i< k$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: x_k is annihilated by L^*.

nodes.name: Normalization
nodes.statement: Multiplying $x_{k}$ by a suitable positive constant, we may additionally assume that $x^*_{k}(x_{k})=1$. Then $\|x_{k}\|\ge 1$ because $x^*_{k}$ has unit norm.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Normalize x_k^*(x_k)=1, so norm of x_k >= 1.

nodes.name: Remaining bound
nodes.statement: To finish the inductive step it suffices to check that $\|x_k\|<4$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Remains to show norm of x_k < 4.

nodes.name: Norm bound
nodes.statement: Assuming the converse, find a functional $x^*\in X^*$ with unit norm such that $x^*(x_k)=\|x_k\|\ge 4$. Then the functional $y^*=x^*_k-\frac14x^*$ belongs to the ball $B^*$ and thus $y^*(x_k)>0$. On the other hand, $y^*(x_k)=x^*_k(x_k)-\frac14x^*(x_k)\le 1-\frac14\cdot4= 0$, which is a desired contradiction.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: A norming functional would yield an element of the ball with non-positive value, contradiction.

nodes.name: Biorthogonal sequence
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l6.1}, there exists a biorthogonal sequence $\{(x_n,x_n^*)\}_{n\in\omega}\subset X\times V^*_C$ such that $1=\|x_n^*\|\le \|x_n\|<4$ for all $n\in\omega$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Take the biorthogonal sequence of Lemma 6.1.

nodes.name: Define C_eps
nodes.statement: Then for every $\varepsilon>0$, a positively hiding convex set $C_\varepsilon$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)\le\varepsilon$ can be defined by the formula: $$C_\varepsilon=\big\{x\in \mathrm{cl}(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B):\forall n\in\omega\;\;x^*_n(x)\le \tfrac18\varepsilon+\sup x^*_n(C)\big\}$$where $\mathbb B=\{x\in X:\|x\|<1\}$ stands for the open unit ball of the Banach space $X$. It is clear that $C\subset C_\varepsilon\subset \mathrm{cl}(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B)$, which implies that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C,C)\le\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Cut the closed eps-neighbourhood by half-spaces.

nodes.name: Remaining
nodes.statement: It remains to check that the set $\tilde C$ is positively hiding. This can be done as follows.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Remains to show positive hiding.

nodes.name: Points a_n
nodes.statement: For every $n\in\omega$ choose a point $c_n\in C$ with $x^*_n(c_n)>\sup x^*_n(C)-\tfrac1{16}\varepsilon$ and consider the point $a_n=c_n+\frac{\varepsilon}4 x_n$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Choose near-maximizers c_n and set a_n=c_n+(eps/4)x_n.

nodes.name: Distance of a_n
nodes.statement: We claim that $\mathsf{dist}(a_n,C_\varepsilon)\ge \frac1{16}\varepsilon$. Indeed, for any point $c\in C_\varepsilon$, we get $x^*_n(c)\le\sup x^*_n(C)+\frac18\varepsilon$ while $$x^*_n(a_n)=\frac\varepsilon4 x^*_n(x_n)+x^*_n(c_n)>\frac\varepsilon4+\sup x^*_n(C)-\frac\varepsilon{16}=\frac{3\varepsilon}{16}+\sup x^*_n(C).$$ Consequently, $\|a_n^*-c\|=\|x^*_n\|\cdot\|a_n-c\|\ge x^*_n(a_n)-x^*(c)\ge \frac{3\varepsilon}{16}-\frac{\varepsilon}{8}=\frac\varepsilon{16}$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Claim each a_n is eps/16 away from C_eps.

nodes.name: Compare functionals
nodes.statement: Indeed, for any point $c\in C_\varepsilon$, we get $x^*_n(c)\le\sup x^*_n(C)+\frac18\varepsilon$ while $$x^*_n(a_n)=\frac\varepsilon4 x^*_n(x_n)+x^*_n(c_n)>\frac\varepsilon4+\sup x^*_n(C)-\frac\varepsilon{16}=\frac{3\varepsilon}{16}+\sup x^*_n(C).$$
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Compare x_n^* on C_eps and on a_n.

nodes.name: Distance bound
nodes.statement: Consequently, $\|a_n^*-c\|=\|x^*_n\|\cdot\|a_n-c\|\ge x^*_n(a_n)-x^*(c)\ge \frac{3\varepsilon}{16}-\frac{\varepsilon}{8}=\frac\varepsilon{16}$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Obtain the eps/16 bound.

nodes.name: Positive distance
nodes.statement: So, the set $A=\{a_n\}_{n\in\omega}$ lies on positive distance $\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C_\varepsilon)\ge\frac1{16}\varepsilon$ from $C_\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: A is at positive distance from C_eps.

nodes.name: Midpoint reduction
nodes.statement: To show that the set $A$ is infinite and hidden behind $C_\varepsilon$, it suffices to check that for any distinct numbers $n,m$ the midpoint $\frac12a_n+\frac12a_m$ of the segment $[a_n,a_m]$ belongs to the convex set $C_\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Reduce hiding to midpoints lying in C_eps.

nodes.name: Midpoint in neighbourhood
nodes.statement: Taking into account that $a_n,a_m\subset \mathrm{cl}(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B)$, we conclude that $\frac12a_n+\frac12a_m\in [a_n,a_m]\subset \mathrm{cl}(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B)$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: The midpoint lies in the eps-neighbourhood.

nodes.name: Check constraints
nodes.statement: The inclusion $\frac12a_n+\frac12a_m\in C_\varepsilon$ will follow from definition of $C_\varepsilon$ as soon as we check that $x^*_k(\frac12a_n+\frac12a_m)\le\sup x^*_k(C)+\frac18\varepsilon$ for every $k\in\omega$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to checking each functional constraint.

nodes.name: k outside {n,m}
nodes.statement: If $k\notin\{n,m\}$, then $x^*_k(x_n)=x^*_k(x_m)=0$ and hence $$x^*_k(\tfrac12a_n+\tfrac12a_m)=x^*_k(\tfrac12c_n+\tfrac12c_m)\le\sup x^*_k(C).$$
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Biorthogonality makes the constraint hold.

nodes.name: k=n or k=m
nodes.statement: If $k=n$, then $$x^*_k(\tfrac12a_n+\tfrac12a_m)=x^*_n(\tfrac12c_n+\tfrac12c_m)+\tfrac18\varepsilon x^*_n(x_n)\le\sup x^*_n(C)+\tfrac18\varepsilon.$$By analogy we can treat the case $k=m$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Direct estimate; k=m by symmetry.

nodes.name: Reduce to pointed cone
nodes.statement: Using Lemma~\ref{l3.3} (by analogy with the proof of Lemma~\ref{l3.4}), we can reduce the proof to the case $-V_C\cap V_C=\{0\}$. So, from now on we assume that $-V_C\cap V_C=\{0\}$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.3 assume the cone is pointed.

nodes.name: Non-empty interior
nodes.statement: Replacing $C$ by a shift of its closed neighborhood, we can assume that $C$ has non-empty interior $C_0$ in $X$ and $0\in C_0$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: WLOG C has interior containing 0.

nodes.name: Non-polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: If the characteristic cone $V_C$ is not polyhedral in its closed linear hull $Z=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$, then by Lemma~\ref{l5.3}, the convex set $C$ is infinitely (and hence positively) hiding and hence we can put $C_\varepsilon=C$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.3 makes C infinitely hiding; take C_eps=C.

nodes.name: Polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: So, we assume that the characteristic cone $V_C$ is polyhedral in $Z$. Since $-V_C\cap V_C=\{0\}$, the polyhedrality of $V_C$ implies that the closed linear space $Z=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$ is finite-dimensional and coincides with $V_C-V_C$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Then Z=V_C-V_C is finite-dimensional.

nodes.name: Quotient by Z
nodes.statement: Now consider the quotient Banach space $\tilde X=X/Z$, the quotient operator $q:X\to\tilde X$, and the convex set $\tilde C=q(C)$. Since the operator $q$ is open, the image $\tilde C_0=q(C_0)$ of the interior $C_0$ of $C$ coincides with the interior of $\tilde C$. Now consider the characteristic cone $V_{\tilde C_0}$ of the open convex set $\tilde C_0$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Pass to X/Z and the cone of the image interior.

nodes.name: Non-trivial quotient cone
nodes.statement: If $V_{\tilde C_0}$ contains some non-zero vector $\tilde v$, then for any vector $v\in q^{-1}(v)$ and for the finite-dimensional linear subspace $E=\mathrm{lin}(Z\cup\{v\})$ the intersection $E\cap C_0$ lies on infinite Hausdorff distance $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(E\cap C_0,V_{E\cap C_0})=\infty$ from its characteristic cone. This is so because $q(V_{E\cap C_0})\subset q(V_C)=\{0\}$ while $q(E\cap C_0)\supset\bar{\mathbb R}_+\tilde v$. Then Lemma~\ref{l5.8} guarantees that the set $C$ is infinitely (and hence positively) hiding. In this case we can put $C_\varepsilon=C$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.13 makes C infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Trivial quotient cone
nodes.statement: So, it remains to consider the case $V_{\tilde C_0}=\{0\}$. In this case, Lemma~\ref{l6.2} yields a positively hiding closed convex set $\tilde C_\varepsilon\subset\tilde X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(\tilde C_\varepsilon,\tilde C_0)<\varepsilon$. Now consider the convex set $C_\varepsilon=(C+\varepsilon\mathbb B)\cap q^{-1}(\tilde C_\varepsilon)$ and observe that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)\le\varepsilon$ and $q(C_\varepsilon)=\tilde C_\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.2 approximates the quotient; pull back.

nodes.name: Hidden set downstairs
nodes.statement: The set $\tilde C_\varepsilon$, being positively hiding, hides a countably infinite set $\tilde A\subset \tilde X\setminus\tilde C_\varepsilon$ on positive distance $\inf_{a\in\tilde A}\mathsf{dist}(a,\tilde C_\varepsilon)>0$ from $\tilde C_\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Take the hidden set of the quotient approximation.

nodes.name: Lift by Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: Taking into account that $Z=V_{Z\cap C_0}-V_{Z\cap C_0}$ and $q(C_\varepsilon)=\tilde C_\varepsilon$, with help of Lemma~\ref{l5.4}, we can find an infinite subset $A\subset q^{-1}(\tilde A)$ hidden behind the convex set $C_\varepsilon\subset C$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Lift it by Lemma 5.4.

nodes.name: Positive distance
nodes.statement: Since the quotient operator $q$ is not expanding, the set $A$ lies on positive distance $$\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C)=\inf_{a\in A}\mathsf{dist}(a,C_0)\ge\inf_{\tilde a\in\tilde A}\mathsf{dist}(\tilde a,\tilde C_0)>0$$from the convex set $C_\varepsilon$. So, $C_\varepsilon$ is positively hiding.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Non-expansion keeps the distance positive.

nodes.name: Infinite codimension
nodes.statement: If the closed linear subspace $V_C^\pm=\mathrm{cl}(V_C-V_C)$ has infinite codimension in $X$, then the existence of a positively hiding convex set $C_\varepsilon\subset X$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C_\varepsilon,C)<\varepsilon$ follows from Lemma~\ref{l6.3}.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.3 applies.

nodes.name: Finite codimension
nodes.statement: So, we assume that $V^\pm_C$ has finite codimension in $X$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Assume finite codimension.

nodes.name: Non-polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: If the characteristic cone $V_C$ is not polyhedral in $V_C^\pm$, then the set $C$ is infinitely (and positively) hiding by Lemma~\ref{l5.3}. In this case we can put $C_\varepsilon=C$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.3 makes C infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: It remains to consider the case of polyhedral cone $V_C$ in $V_C^\pm$. Since $V_C^\pm$ has finite codimension in $X$, the characteristic cone $V_C$ is polyhedral in $X$ and hence the closed linear subspace $V^\mp_C=-V_C\cap V_C$ has finite codimension in $X$.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: The lineality space has finite codimension.

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional quotient
nodes.statement: Then the quotient Banach space $Y=X/V^\mp_C$ is finite-dimensional. Let $q:X\to Y$ be the quotient operator. Lemma~\ref{l3.3} guarantees that $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(qC,V_{qC})=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)=\infty$ and then the set $qC$ is infinitely hiding in $Y$ by Lemma~\ref{l5.8}.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 3.3 and 5.13 make qC infinitely hiding.

nodes.name: Lift by Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l5.5}, the set $C$ is infinitely (and hence positively) hiding in $X$. Letting $C_\varepsilon=C$, we finish the proof of the lemma.
nodes.section: 6 Approximating by positively hiding convex sets
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.5 lifts infinite hiding to C.

nodes.name: Restate conditions
nodes.statement: To prove the first part of Theorem~\ref{main}, for every closed convex subset $C$ of a Banach space $X$ we should prove the equivalence of the following conditions: \begin{enumerate} \item $C$ is approximatively polyhedral; \item the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ is polyhedral in $X$ and $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)<\infty$; \item $\mathcal H_C$ contains a polyhedral closed convex set; \item $\mathcal H_C$ contains no positively hiding closed convex set; \item the space $\mathcal H_C$ is separable; \item the space $\mathcal H_C$ has density $\mathrm{dens}(\mathcal H_C)<\mathfrak c$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Restate conditions (1)-(6).

nodes.name: Implication scheme
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the implications $(1)\Rightarrow(2)\Rightarrow(3)\Rightarrow(5)\Rightarrow(6)\Rightarrow(4)\Rightarrow(2)\Rightarrow(3)\Rightarrow(1)$, among which $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$ and $(5)\Rightarrow(6)$ are trivial. The remaining implications can be established as follows. \smallskip
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a cycle of implications, two trivial.

nodes.name: (1) implies (2): cones agree
nodes.statement: To prove the implication $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$, assume that the closed convex set $C$ is approximatively polyhedral and find a polyhedral convex set $P$ with $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)<\infty$. Lemma~\ref{l2.4n} implies that $V_C=V_P$.
nodes.statement_short: A polyhedral P at finite distance has V_P=V_C by Lemma 2.4.

nodes.name: (1) implies (2): polyhedral cone
nodes.statement: The polyhedral convex set $P$ can be written as a finite intersection $P=\bigcap_{i=1}^n f_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,a_i]\big)$ of closed hyperplanes determined by some functionals $f_1,\dots,f_n:X\to\mathbb R$ and some real numbers $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R$. It is easy to check that $$V_C=V_P=\bigcap_{i=1}^n f_i^{-1}\big((-\infty,0]\big),$$ which means that the characteristic cone $V_C$ of $C$ is polyhedral.
nodes.statement_short: V_P is the intersection of the homogeneous half-spaces.

nodes.name: (1) implies (2): finite distance
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{l2.6}, $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P,V_C)=\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P,V_P)<\infty$. Consequently, $\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,V_C)\le \mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(C,P)+\mathsf{d}_{\mathsf H}\kern-1pt(P,V_C)<\infty$. \smallskip
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.6 and the triangle inequality give finite distance.

nodes.name: Remaining implications
nodes.statement: The implications $(3)\Rightarrow(5)$ and $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$ are proved in Lemma~\ref{l3.4} and $(6)\Rightarrow(4)$ in Lemmas~\ref{l4.2}. The implication $(4)\Rightarrow(2)$ follows from Lemmas~\ref{l5.3}, \ref{l6.3} and \ref{l6.4}.

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional part
nodes.statement: Next, assuming the Banach space is finite-dimensional we will check that the conditions (1)--(6) are equivalent to: \begin{enumerate} \item[(7)] $C$ is not positively hiding; \item[(8)] $C$ is not infinitely hiding. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Restate conditions (7),(8).

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional implications
nodes.statement: It suffices to check that $(4)\Rightarrow(7)\Rightarrow(8)\Rightarrow (2)$. In fact, the first two implications $(4)\Rightarrow(7)\Rightarrow(8)$ are trivial, while $(8)\Rightarrow(2)$ follows from Lemmas~\ref{l5.3} and \ref{l5.8}.
